Instructor: One thing I wanna call out explicitly
is the idea of using locks in relational databases.
That is something that shows up on the exam
guide, so we better talk about it.
One way of doing that is using the Lock command.
So the idea of locks is preventing two people from doing the
same thing at the same
time to something, right?
And getting conflicting results as a result.
So implicitly relational databases will lock your tables to prevent
that from happening.
So you don't want two people writing at the same
time to the same piece of data, right?
And you also don't want people reading
data while that write is in process to that bit of data.
So generally to ensure acid compliance, databases will automatically
and implicitly lock things
to prevent that sort of thing from
happening.
You don't really need to do anything special about that.
However, it is possible to explicitly lock tables or explicitly
lock rows to ensure your own data integrity and concurrency control,
if you don't wanna just put your
faith in the database to do
the right thing.
There could be some special circumstances
where you want more explicit control over those locks.
So there's two kinds of locks.
There's what's called a Shared Lock and an Exclusive Lock.
So the syntax for a shared lock is For Share.
We'll see an example of that on the next slide.
But a shared lock allow to reads, but prevents writes.
And it can be held by multiple transactions.
So if you want to allow people to read the data
that's being accessed by your transaction,
but prevent people from writing
to it during your transaction,
you can say For Share to enforce a shared lock.
You can also have an exclusive lock that prevents all
reads and writes to a resource.
And only one transaction can hold
an exclusive lock at a time.
That's why it's called Exclusive.
The syntax for that is For Update.
And that says, "While I'm accessing this data, nobody
can read it, nobody can write to it,
nobody can look at it or touch it but me. Some examples, and these are in MySQL,
the syntax again varies from database to database,
so don't get too hung up on the syntax,
but if you wanted to lock an entire
table, you could say Lock Tables, employees,
where employees is the name of the table
I want to lock.
Right, that would lock the entire employee's table
against being written to.
And when I'm done,
I would have to say Unlock Table to release that lock.

So if I want to make sure nobody
can write to my table while I'm doing something, Lock Tables
is the way to do it.

Also an example of doing a Shared Lock.

# 89. Redshift Distribution Styles
# Section: Database
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40356010
# Caption: en_US (auto)

When we discussed the redshift architecture, we talked about how the data in your table is distributed
across many compute nodes and many slices within those nodes.
Now, there are several different ways of actually doing that distribution that you need to understand.
So when data is loaded into a table, redshift will distribute the table's rows to the compute nodes and
slices according to the distribution style that you chose when you created the table.
The two primary goals of data distribution are to distribute the workload uniformly among
the nodes in the cluster, and to minimize data movement during query execution.
There are four different distribution styles and they are as follows.
Auto distribution.
If you don't specify a distribution style, Amazon Redshift uses auto distribution, and based
on the size of the table data, redshift will assign an optimal distribution style for you, and
that might be even key or all.
So let's dive into each one of those independently.
First let's talk about even distribution.
So an even distribution regardless of the values in any particular column, the leader node distributes
the rows across the slices in a round robin fashion.
So it's just going to step through each individual slice and keep assigning new data to each slice
in a circular manner.
This is appropriate when a table does not participate in joins, or when there is not a clear choice
between key distribution or all distribution.
So even distribution just tries to spread things out as evenly as possible without thinking about trying
to cluster data together that might be accessed at the same time.
Key distribution.
Here the rows are distributed according to the values in one column, so the leader node will place matching
values on the same node.
Slice and matching values from the common columns are physically stored together, so this can come in handy
if you're typically going to be doing queries based on a specific column in your data.
By using key distribution, you can make sure that all the data associated with a specific key value
will be physically located on the same slice, and that can speed up your queries.
So the diagram here is showing you that as new rows are coming in from your incoming data, those keys will
be hashed and set to a specific slice based on how that key is hashed.
Then we have all distribution, and with all distribution, a copy of the entire table is distributed
to every node.
That ensures that every row is co-located.
For every join that the table participates in, the all distribution multiplies the storage required
by the number of nodes in the cluster, so it takes much longer to load, update, or insert data into multiple
tables.
All distribution is really only appropriate for relatively slow moving tables, that is, tables that
are not updated frequently or extensively.
As the cost of redistribution is low, small dimension tables do not benefit significantly from all
distribution.
Now, if you ever need to view the distribution style of a table, you can query the PG class
info view or the SV table info view.
The Reflective Style column in PG class info will indicate the current distribution style for that table.

# 92. Redshift Resizing
# Section: Database
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40356046
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: So what if concurrency scaling isn't enough
and you need to actually resize your cluster on the fly,
you need to add more capacity to it?
Well, there's a few ways of doing that,
and you need to understand the difference between them.
So one is called elastic resize.
You can use this to quickly add or remove nodes
of the same type.
So if you're happy with the type of nodes,
the type of EC2 instances
that are running your Redshift cluster,
you can add more or remove them using elastic resize.
With elastic resize,
your cluster will only be down for a few minutes
while it adds that capacity,
and it tries to actually keep those connections open
across the downtime as well,
so you might not even drop any queries,
it might just keep that connection held open
and let it resume
once that added capacity is in place on your cluster.
Now, one limit of elastic resize is that for certain dc2
and ra3 node types, you're limited to either doubling
or halving the size of that cluster.
You don't really need to remember
what the specific types are for the exam,
but for certain types, that is what you need to do,
you can only double or halve them.
If you need to do something a little bit more involved,
then you need to go back to what's called classic resize,
and that allows you to actually change the node types
and/or the number of nodes.
The thing with classic resize
is that if you're actually changing the node types,
it could take hours or even days
for your cluster to become writeable again.
So your cluster will be in a read-only state
for the entire period of time
that it takes to provision that new hardware
and swap it out in your cluster.
That can be a very lengthy experience.
So you wanna use elastic resize when you can,
but if you need to change your node type,
you have to use classic resize.
That's the main difference there.
One technique for dealing with things
in that classic resize scenario
is to use what's called snapshot, restore, resize.
And this is a strategy for keeping your cluster available
during a classic resize operation.
So if you do need to change your node type
or you need to add a amount of capacity
that elastic resize won't allow you to do,
what you can do is use a snapshot command
to make a copy of your cluster,
and then resize that new cluster.
So your data's still going to the old cluster
while your new cluster is being resized
and going through the classic resize process.
Once your new cluster is finally done,
you can then shift your traffic
to that new cluster that's been created.
So snapshot, restore, then resize is a way of migrating
from one cluster to another using classic resize
to minimize downtime.

# 96. Redshift Materialized Views
# Section: Database
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40394256
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: You need
to know about materialized views for the exam as well.
Let's talk about what those are in Redshift.
So you know what a view is in a database,
it's just basically taking the results of a query and
making that look like another table
you can query subsequently.
A materialized view is a little bit different.
So it's actually pre-computing the results of that query and
storing the results of that query and
making that look like another table.
So it's different from a normal view, if you will,
in that it's actually storing the results of the query
and not just the query itself.
So as you can see, this might be a pretty important performance
optimization.
So if you have a complex query in your data warehouse on
a large table, you can query that materialized view just
like any other table or view based on
those saved results from a more complex query.
So if you need to build a query on top of
some more complicated query, you can store the results
of that complicated query
into a materialized view and
then query those results repeatedly from other queries.
So since you're using those pre-computed results
and not accessing the base tables, that can
be a very important performance optimization.
Of course, it comes at the cost
of having a synchronization problem.
So if the results of your materialized view change because the
underlying stuff that you're a querying changes, that materialized
view needs to be explicitly refreshed
somehow.
So an example of where you might wanna use
this is if you have a predictable and recurring
query, like populating a dashboard from Amazon QuickSight
or something like that.
So if you know your dashboard is
going to need the results of a given set of queries,
maybe you can pre-compute those results
using materialized views and then
build your dashboard against
that materialized view to make it more performant instead
of running that query every
time you wanna look at your dashboard.
How do I use them? They're pretty easy.
So instead of create
view, you just say, create a materialized view and that's it.
So instead of a view that's based on the query,
you're creating a snapshot of the results of that query
and making a view out of it.
How do I keep 'em refreshed?
So like I said, there's a synchronization problem
because I'm storing the results
and not just the query itself.
There might be a synchronization
issue where the underlying data that I'm querying that materialized
view from changes.
So to keep the materialized view in sync with those
changes, I can manually and explicitly refresh that
when I need to by using the refresh materialized view command.
You can also set the auto refresh option
when you're creating
it to just make that happen automatically.
So it depends how much control you want over it.
If you wanna have a control over how often
it's being refreshed to maintain performance, maybe
you only need to refresh it once a day because you're gonna be
using this for a dashboard
that's queried once a day.
Then maybe just refresh that materialized view once a day as
opposed to automatically refreshing
it every time something changes.
Once you have a materialized view,
you can query it just like any other table or view.
It looks just like anything else, and
you can also stack them on top of each other.
So you can have materialized views
that are built from other materialized views,
which is pretty cool.
An example of where that might be useful
is, if you have some expensive JOIN operation
among multiple tables, you could store the results of
that JOIN as a materialized view, and then have
other materialized views that have
specific queries using that joined data.
So you can stack them on top of each other as well,
which can also be used to accelerate your query performance.

These are generated from logs that are persisted to disc
and then there are SVCS views,
which are details about queries
on both main and concurrency scaling clusters.
For specifically queries on main clusters,
SVL views will have that information.
And the specific tables and views
that are available will vary based on
whether you're using a provision instance
or a serverless instance,
but they do have a lot in common.
Let's take a look at this example on the right here.
So here's an example,
where we're analyzing the execution time of recent queries.
So if we kind of break it down here,
we can see that we're getting this from stl_query, right?
So stl_query is an STL view.
That means that's generated from logs persisted to disk,
and we're joining that on svl_qlog.
So again, SVL is details about queries on main clusters,
so svl_qlog would probably be the query log, right?
We're doing a join there between those two,
based on the query field there.
So we're joining up svl_qlog
with stl_query to get those recent queries
and specifically saying we're doing a WHERE clause
to get it within the past one day, right?
So by getting that information on recent queries,
we can then select the attributes of those queries,
like the start time, the end time,
how long that time took,
we're gonna compute that
and compute the execution time using the DATEDIFF command
and the status of that at the end.
So just an example of using system tables
and system views for getting some information about
how Redshift is performing for you.

# 101. Redshift Data API
# Section: Database
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/45598863
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Something that seems to be coming up more on the exam is the Redshift Data API.
So let's spend a little bit of time talking about that in some detail.
It is a secure HTTP endpoint for SQL statements to your redshift cluster.
And that can be a provisioned cluster or a serverless cluster.
And that can handle both individual and batch queries.
So so it offers, among other things, a Rest endpoint that you can integrate with your own applications.
And that's what we're illustrating on the bottom of the screen here.
So you can have users talking to some application that you've built.
That application can then go through the AWS SDK and call the Amazon Redshift Data API through it and
through that API, execute queries against your redshift cluster wherever it might be.
So let's you use that outside of AWS.
Potentially it is asynchronous.
So you'll make a call to request a query either in a batch or an individual query.
And then you have to make another call with the identifier that it gives back to you to retrieve the
results of that later on.
It does not require managing connections like you would with a normal database, so you don't need to
worry about having the right drivers installed on your application or anything like that.
It's all abstracted away from you through the data API.
And from a security standpoint, you don't have to worry.
Passwords are not sent through the API either.
It uses either AWS Secrets Manager to manage credentials, or you can set up temporary credentials in
redshift for your application.
Either way, the password is not sent across the wire as part of the API, and because it can be invoked
by the AWS SDK, that means you can access redshift through any language supported by the SDK that includes
C plus plus, go, Java, JavaScript.
Net, Node.js, PHP, Python, and Ruby.
And as with most services, it integrates with CloudTrail.
So if you need to monitor what's going on or archive what's being performed through that API, CloudTrail
can capture those API calls for you and store them in S3 somewhere.
And it's not just for application integration.
It also integrates with many other services within the AWS ecosystem.
And they're all visualized here on the right here.
So like I said, we can use the Rest endpoint to integrate it with your own application.
That's what we talked about.
But you can also integrate it with a variety of other services.
And a very popular one would be using AWS Step Functions together with Redshift Data API to orchestrate
a ETL process, extract, transform and load.
So if you want to set up a data processing workflow using step functions, you can call Redshift Data
API as part of that workflow and set up an event driven ETL pipeline using data API.
You can also access Redshift Data API through a SageMaker notebook.
So if you need to hit redshift from a SageMaker notebook, you can do that as well.
And it also integrates with Amazon EventBridge.
And this is an important one in the context of data engineering.
So you can stream data from the data API to someplace else using EventBridge by monitoring the data
coming out of the data API.
So you could, for example, stream that data from an application to Lambda by streaming that data using
EventBridge.
And to do that, you would just set the width event parameter to true.
To accomplish that kind of streaming, you can also schedule data API operations using EventBridge.
So EventBridge can be used to schedule operations on a consistent schedule or in response to some sort
of other event.
So EventBridge Plus data API is something you should know about some finer points on using the data
API.
So there's a bunch of maximum limits on what you can do with it.
And by default, the query duration can only last for 24 hours.
You can only have 500 active queries at a time.
The result size, which is gzipped, can only be up to 100MB.
The result will only be retained for 24 hours.
So if you don't get it after a full day, it's going to be gone.
Your query statement size can only be 100kB, and this next one is a little bit more important the packet
for query size.
That's the amount of data per row in your results is 64kB.
So if you were to get back an error message from your data API call saying that packet for query is
too large, it's telling you that there's too much information per row in the data that you're retrieving,
and that maximum limit is 64kB.
Also, there's an eight hour maximum retention time for client tokens for accessing the API, and there
are various TPS quotas per API call.
For example, for execute statement.
You're limited to 30 transactions per statement.
Speaking of API calls, these are the ones you have available to you.
There's both execute statement for executing a single SQL statement or batch execute statement for executing
multiple ones at once.
And once you have that statement submitted, you can describe the statement or the table behind it.
And again this is a synchronous.
So once you call an execute statement call or batch execute statement call it's going to just give you
back an identifier not the actual result.
So you then need to turn around and pass that identifier back into get statement result to later retrieve
the result of that query.
You can also cancel a statement that's in progress using cancel statement using that same ID.
And there is some security around making sure that you can't snoop in on other people's queries.
So you do need to have the same IAM role or permission to operate on a given statement across execute
and get statement, result or what have you.
So you can't go and get a statement result for somebody else's execute statement call for example.
Obviously also the cluster must be in a VPC.
So unless your redshift cluster is in a virtual private cloud, it won't work.

Okay, so now let's talk about AWS Snowball.
So it's a highly secure and portable device
that allows you to collect and process data
at the edge and migrate data in and out of AWS.
So if you have a migration of say, petabytes of data,
Snowball may be a good use case.
So we have two kind of Snowball edge devices.
One is called the Edge Storage Optimized,
and the other one is called the Edge Compute Optimized.
And the difference lies in their storage.
As you can see, one has 210 terabytes
and the other one has 28 terabytes.
So obviously one is for storage
and the other one is only used for computer.
So let me tell you about data migrations.
So it takes a lot of time to transfer some data
over a specific bandwidth speed.
For example, if you want to transfer a hundred terabytes
over one gigabytes per second connection,
it would take you 12 days.
So when you have a slow connection,
you may have limited connectivity, limited bandwidth,
very high network cost, and you have to share the bandwidth,
for example, with some other applications,
the connection may not be stable.
So whenever you have these kind of challenges,
or if it takes you, for example, over a week
to transfer data over the network,
the recommendation is to use a Snowball device.
So the idea is that if you upload directly to Amazon S3,
it's simple, but it may use all your bandwidth.
And if you use Snowball,
well, you're going to receive a physical Snowball device,
you, yourself in your own infrastructure.
So it's a physical machine,
and then you load it with the data you need,
and then finally you ship it back to AWS.
And then you will be having an export process
within AWS to take your data from the Snowball onto,
for example, an Amazon S3 bucket.
So this is the main use case of a Snowball device.
The other one is a edge computing use case.
So the idea is that you wanna process data
while it's being created on an edge location.
For example, it's a truck on the road or a ship on the sea,
or a mining station on the ground.
And these locations may have no internet access
or limited access to internet or compute power.
So here again, we order one of these
big Snowball edge devices and we do edge computing.
And so that means that we have the Compute Optimized,
this is dedicated for that use case
for the search optimized devices.
And then because they have computing capability,
we can actually run EC2 instances
or Lambda functions directly on these devices.
The idea is that once the data is created
and processed, we can send it back again to AWS,
but by using an edge computing device,
we can pre-process the data
or we can do machine learning at the edge
or directly transcode media at the edge.
And that's the use case for edge computing.
So hopefully that makes sense.
The Snowball service is really just something that is used
for data migrations and edge computing.
Alright, that's it, I hope you liked it

then you can go as big as you want
for size, it's durable, it's dynamic.
The storage type is object, so you need to use the S3 API
to access the Amazon S3 objects.
And then you have atomic operations,
so you can get, put, post and so on with versioning.
For the pricing, you pay, of course for Amazon S3 pricing,
so storage plus request, plus data transfer,
and to get access to Amazon S3, you need
to make sure you have the proper IAM permissions.
This is network based storage, so we'll have a fast access
because we have dedicated AWS bandwidth,
but it's not the fastest.
And of course, Amazon is free, it is shared
across all your Lambda invocations because, well,
it is an external storage of data.
Finally, for Amazon EFS, we have elastic.
It's durable, it's dynamic.
The storage type is file systems, so we access it
using any kind of file system operation.
We're going to pay for the storage,
the data transfer, and the throughput.
And because it is mounted
as a network file system on your Lambda function,
you're going to have very fast access to your data.
Finally, because it is a network file system, this is going
to be shared across all your Lambda invocations.
So hopefully that makes sense
into the different storage options for Lambda.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 118. AWS SAM
# Section: Compute
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305348
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS SAM.
So SAM is this little squirrel,
but it's also the Serverless Application Model.
It's an actual framework to develop
and deploy serverless applications.
So that means that you write your code
and then you're going to use a configuration
in the YAML format, which is going
to be compliant with the SAM framework.
And automatically, SAM is going to generate
very complex CloudFormation files
from simple SAM YAML files.
It supports anything from CloudFormation.
So you can still use outputs, mappings, parameter,
resources, et cetera in your SAM YAML code.
Now, SAM behind the scene can also use CodeDeploy
to deploy Lambda functions,
and SAM can help you run Lambda, API Gateway,
and DynamoDB locally.
So SAM really is intended
to be focused on serverless applications
and allow you to debug them locally
and to deploy them very quickly using CloudFormation
into the AWS cloud.
So SAM is made of recipes,
and at the very top of your template,
you're going to add a transform header
to indicate it's a SAM template.
And this is a transform header
which is going to tell CloudFormation to transform it
into a CloudFormation template.
Then you write your code,
but instead of using the CloudFormation constructs,
you're going to use the SAM constructs,
such as a serverless function, which is a Lambda function,
a serverless API, which is going to be the API gateway,
and the serverless SimpleTable,
which is going to be DynamoDB.
But you have these constructs to make it simpler
and easier for you to write your serverless applications.
And then to package and deploy this application onto AWS,
you're going to use the sam deploy command.
And it used to be two commands.
It used to be sam package and then sam deploy.
But now you can just do sam deploy on its own,
and it is going to package it for you as well.
There's also a way to synchronize your changes into
AWS Lambda very quickly using SAM Accelerate,
and the command is sam sync and then minus minus watch.
I'll give you a bit more
information on this in this lecture.
So let's have a look into SAM deployment.
So you have your application code
as well as your SAM template in the YAML format,
and then you're going to build the application
locally using sam build.
It's going to transform into a CloudFormation template
and your application code,
and then you can deploy it using sam deploy.
So you'll zip and upload everything into an S3 bucket,
and then automatically execute
or ChangeSet against CloudFormation.
Then your CloudFormation stack can be made
of different serverless components such as Lambda,
API Gateway, and DynamoDB.
So let's talk about SAM Accelerate.
So SAM Accelerate is its set of features that is used
to reduce the latency while deploying resources to AWS.
So you want to deploy as fast as possible.
And the command is going to be sam sync
to declare your project,
declare it with a SAM template into AWS.
And it's actually going to bypass CloudFormation
if you just do code changes
without updating your infrastructure
by using the service API.
So it's going to be a very, very quick deployment.
So you have SAM template and your application code,
and your Lambda function already deployed
and you're going to run sam sync.
And automatically, as you change the application code,
automatically SAM is going to synchronize its code
with your Lambda function.
Therefore, if you wanted to test your Lambda function
in the cloud, it's going to be very easy and very quick.
So different options, you can just run sam sync
to synchronize the code and the infrastructure,
or sam sync and just the code option
to synchronize only the code and not the infrastructure.
So you're not going to use CloudFormation,
it's going to be like the updates will be done in seconds.
Then you can specify a specific resource to say, hey,
I only want to update my Lambda functions
and their dependencies,
or I want to update this specific Lambda function
using the resource ID.
Or you can use the watch option,
which is going to monitor for file changes.
So it's going to run in the background
and automatically synchronize anything
when changes are detected.
So if you include configuration, use sam sync,
or if it's just a code,
then it's going to be using sam sync
and then the code option.
So I hope that makes sense.
I hope this is a good overview of SAM.
We'll do some hands-on to practice as well
so it becomes clear for you how it works.
So I hope you like this lecture
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 121. AWS Batch
# Section: Compute
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40356120
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: The next service you need to know
at a high level is AWS Batch.
AWS Batch allows you to run Batch jobs
that its name indicates,
and they're based on Docker images.
And so with AWS Batch, you don't provision the instance.
There's a dynamic provisioning of the instances for you,
whether it's an EC2 instance or a Spot instance.
And Batch figures out the optimal quantity
and the type of these instances
based on the volume of jobs it has to do
and the requirements.
So you don't need to manage any clusters.
It's a fully serverless service, just like Glue,
you just pay for the underlying EC2 instances
that are created by Batch itself.
So you can schedule Batch jobs using CloudWatch Events
to allow you to maybe run on a schedule,
or you can orchestrate Batch job using Step Functions.
And we'll see this in the next lecture.
But, so a question you may have again is,
"What is the difference between Batch and Glue?"
So Glue, again, just to go over it one more time,
it's Apache Spark Code, Scala or Python only,
and it's focused on the ETL.
And you don't worry about configuring managing resources
and you have the data catalog.
Now for Batch, it is a bit different.
It's for any computing job, regardless of the job, okay?
It's not just for ETL,
it's for anything that is Batch oriented.
So as long as you have a Docker image that works for Batch,
you can do it in Batch.
So for example, a job that may be good for Batch,
it would be a cleanup task in an S3 bucket.
So you run a script on an S3 bucket to clean it up,
and you run this as a Batch job every so often.
Whereas in Glue, it's really about taking data,
transforming it, and then placing it somewhere else.
So the resources are created in your accounts
and they're managed by Batch,
so you're using EC2 instances within your account,
so you have access to all the stuff within your accounts.
And so if you have an ETL
means you actually need to transform some data,
Glue is probably going to be a better choice.
But if you have non ETL related work,
but it's still Batch oriented,
then AWS Batch will be better.
So that's it just for this service.
Hope that was helpful
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 123. What is Docker?
# Section: Containers
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305410
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Hello, and welcome to
this section on containers,
where we'll be talking about Docker, ECS and EKS.
So, what is Docker?
Docker is a software development platform to deploy apps.
The idea is that, it's a container technology,
so apps are going to be packaged into containers,
and these containers are sort of standardized,
and so, they can be run on any operating system.
That means that your apps, once they're containerized,
they run the same way, regardless of where they run it.
It could be any machine.
You don't have any compatibility issue.
The behavior is predictable,
which means that you have less work to do.
It's easier to maintain and deploy.
And it should work with any kind of language,
any operating system, and any technology.
So the use cases for Docker are a microservice architecture,
so this is a good keyword to have in mind,
lift-and-shift apps from on-premises to the cloud,
and anytime you wanna run a container, really.
So, how does Docker work on an operating system?
Well, we have a server,
and in our case, it may be EC2 instances,
but it could be any kind of server,
and you're going to run a Docker agent.
And then, from there, you can start Docker containers.
And so, your first Docker container
may contain a Java application.
And your second Docker container
may contain a Node.js application.
And Docker containers, they can run multiple times the same.
So you can have multiple Docker containers
of the same Java application,
or multiple Docker containers
of the same Node.js application.
You can also run databases within Docker,
for example, MySQL, and so on.
So Docker is very versatile.
And from a server perspective,
all these things are Docker containers.
So where do you store Docker images?
Well, you store them in something
called a Docker Repository.
And we have multiple options.
The first one is Docker Hub.
And so, it's a public repository.
And you can find base images for many technologies,
or operating systems, such as Ubuntu, MySQL, and so on.
It's very popular.
And then, for more private integration,
you have Amazon ECR, Amazon Elastic Container Registry,
and you can run your private images on there,
but there's also a public repository option available on ECR
called the Amazon ECR Public Gallery.
Now, how is Docker different from a virtual machine?
Well, Docker is sort of a virtualization technology,
but not exactly.
The purist will try to hit me, if I say this.
So, the resources are shared with the host.
That means that you can share many containers on one server.
So, if you look at the architecture for a VM,
you have the infrastructure,
then you have the host operating system,
then you have a hypervisor, and then you have your apps,
and your guest operating system.
And so, this is how, for example, EC2 works.
For example, when you get an EC2 machine,
it is actually a virtual machine running on a hypervisor.
And so, this allows Amazon to offer many EC2 instances
to many different type of customers.
And all these EC2 instances,
all these virtual machines are going to be separate.
They're not going to share resources,
and they're going to be isolated.
But for a Docker container,
you still have the infrastructure,
and the Host OS, which may be this time, in EC2 instance.
Then you have the Docker Daemon,
and then on top of it, you can have a lot of containers
that can be lightweight,
running on top of the Docker Daemon.
And this allows the containers
to really cohabitate together.
They can actually share networking,
share some data, and so on.
So it's a bit less quote unquote secure,
as a virtual machine, but it allows you
to run more containers on a single server.
And this is why we really like Docker containers.
So how to get started with Docker?
Well, first you have to write a Docker file,
which is defining how your Docker container will look.
So we have a base Docker image, and we add some files,
and then we're going to build it.
And this will become a Docker image.
And that Docker image,
you can store it on a Docker repository.
It's called a Push.
And you push it to either Docker Hub,
which is a public repository,
or Amazon ECR, which is Amazon's version
of Docker repositories.
Then you can pull back these images
from these repositories, and then you would run them.
And when you run a Docker image,
it becomes a Docker container, which runs your code
that you had built from your Docker build.
That is the whole process with Docker.
So how do you do Docker container management on AWS?
Well, the first one is called Amazon ECS.
It's Amazon Elastic Container Service.
It's the own platform of Amazon for Docker management.
We'll have a look at it, in deep dive.
Then we have Amazon EKS,
which is Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service,
which is Amazon's managed version of Kubernetes,
which is an open source project.
We'll have a quick look at it.
We have AWS Fargate,
which is Amazon's own serverless container platform,
and Fargate works both with ECS and EKS.
And we'll do a deep dive of Fargate in this section.
And then we have Amazon ECR, used to store container images,
as I showed you from before.
So we have an overview of how to do Docker,
and what is Docker, and how to do Docker on AWS.
Now, let's do a deep dive onto Amazon, ECS and the rest.

# 124. Amazon ECS
# Section: Containers
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305412
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk about Amazon ECS,
and we're gonna get an overview
into all different aspects of it.
So the first thing I wanna talk to you about
is the EC2 Launch Type.
So ECS stands for Elastic Container Service.
And when you launch Docker Containers on AWS,
you are launching what's called an ECS Task on ECS Cluster.
And an ECS Cluster is made of things.
And with the EC2 Launch Type,
well these things are EC2 instances.
And in that case,
if you use an ECS Cluster with an EC2 Launch Type
you must provision and maintain the infrastructure yourself.
So that means that your Amazon ECS/ ECS Cluster
is going to be composed of multiple EC2 instances.
Now, these instances are a little bit special
because each of them must run the ECS Agent,
and then this Agent is going to register each,
EC2 Instance into the Amazon ECS service
and the specified ECS Cluster.
Now, once you have that in place
then when you start ECS tasks
then AWS is going to be starting or stopping the containers.
That means that whenever we have a new Docker container
it's going to be placed accordingly
on each EC2 Instance over time as you can see right here.
And you can start or stop the ECS task,
and it will be placed automatically.
So that's the EC2 Launch Type,
and Docker containers are placed on Amazon
EC2 instances that we provision in advance, okay?
Now, there's a second launch type called
the Fargate Launch Type.

# 134. Running ETL Jobs with Bookmarks
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40356222
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Running Glue jobs,
there's a few ways to do it.
Again, one is to use a Cron-style time-based schedule,
so if you need to run that on some sort of a fixed schedule,
you can do that, same format as Cron,
or you can have something called job bookmarks.
Again, this is an important thing for the exam.
So a job bookmark is used to persist state from the job run.
So if you need to set things up
so that you don't end up reprocessing the same data,
a bookmark allows you to keep track of where you left off,
so that you can prevent the reprocessing of old data,
and just process that new data when you rerun on a schedule.
So the job bookmark keeps track of where you left off
when you're running your Glue jobs on a schedule.
It works with S3 sources in a variety of formats,
and it can also work with relational databases via JDBC
if your primary keys are in sequential order.
Now that feature only handles new rows, not updated rows.
So you can only use job bookmarks with a relational database
if you are injecting new data as new rows.
If it's going back and updating existing rows,
job bookmarks won't work the way you expect.
Might be an important thing to know.
Also CloudWatch events.
So you can fire off a Lambda function,
or an SNS notification, whatever you wanna do,
when an ETL job in Glue succeeds or fails.
So Glue integrates with CloudWatch
to keep track of what happened
and to potentially notify you based on chained events
through SNS or Lambda, whatever you wanna do,
when that job succeeds or fails.
Once that happens, you can invoke an EC2 run
to do further processing, send the event on to Kinesis,
activate a Step Function, whatever you might wanna do.
So just keep in mind, you know, using CloudWatch,
you can tie together Glue with other systems
like EC2, Kinesis, or AWS Step Functions.

# 136. AWS Glue Flex Jobs
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/54600683
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Something coming up on the exam lately
is Glue Flex jobs.
They're pretty much what they sound like.
So it's a new execution class called FLEX,
that's appropriate for non-urgent workload.
So if you don't really care when your job runs
or necessarily how much capacity it has,
you can run a Flex job to use spare compute capacity
instead of dedicated workers.
And of course, this is a way to save money.
Now, the trade-off is you might have to wait
for that capacity to become available,
or it might not be available at all,
in which case you might get less capacity
than you asked for even.
However, if you have a time-insensitive workload,
maybe you're doing some testing,
or a one-off load, or something on the weekend
where you don't really care when exactly it runs,
you just want it to run sometime in the near future,
a Flex job might be a way to save some money.
How much money? Usually about 30-35%
less than a standard execution job.
You're only going to be billed
for the actual number of workers used
and the duration that they actually ran for.
And again, you might end up with less than you asked for
if the capacity is not available.
Few caveats, though, so you cannot use Flex jobs
with Python shell jobs, with streaming jobs,
or with AWS Glue machine learning jobs
that might be important to remember.
So at a nutshell, at a high level,
if you do need dedicated resources or predictable times
and predictable performance or concrete SLAs,
you want to use a standard glue job.
But if you're willing to trade that off
for saving some bucks, a Flex job might be for you.

relates to Databrew one way of dealing with PII is with substitution.

And substitute that information with something that is not personally identifiable.
I could shuffle it.
I could take all of the PII values in my rows and shuffle them all together so that Person A's credit

Deterministic encryption is one way of encrypting that personally identifiable information in such a

You can also decrypt something that was encrypted using a decrypt command, and there's probably no

The delete transformation can be used to just drop that information entirely.
You can also mask out personally identifiable information.
So a lot of times you'll see only the last four digits of a credit card or a social security number
being displayed where the rest of it is masked out or scrambled in some way.
Masking is a way to do that.
And finally, there's hashing, where you apply some sort of a hash function to the value in a cryptographic
fashion.

So if you are concerned about performance,
make sure that you're using a columnar data format
under the hood with Athena in ORC or Parquet.
So if it's hitting S3 data, if it's in that format already,
it will save you quite a bit of work.
Also, remember, a small number
of large files will generally perform better
than a large number of small files with Athena.
So if you can have a small number
of large-ish columnar data files,
that's probably gonna be
your optimal performance case right there.
Also, take advantage of partitions.
So if you're able to organize your data in S3
in a partition format that lines up
with how you're going to be querying that data,
so for example, if you're hitting up your data most commonly
by a specific date range or something like that,
then partitioning your data
by date would make a lot of sense, right?
Now, if you do need to add partitions after the fact,
let's say that you have an existing data set in S3
that is not partitioned
and you want to improve its performance
by adding partitions,
you don't have to totally start from scratch.
What you can do in Athena
is use a command called MSCK REPAIR TABLE to go back
and add that metadata for the partitions into Athena.
So if you do need to add partitions later on
to an existing Athena database,
you can use MSCK REPAIR TABLE to accomplish that.
So those are the main points about Athena performance.
Just remember those three things,
and you should be in good shape.

# 148. Athena ACID Transactions
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40356400
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: A new feature in Athena
is ACID transaction support.
That means that we have strict guarantees
about transactions.
So you can actually have concurrent users hitting the same
row at the same time and have it all work consistently.
Under the hood is powered by Apache Iceberg.
And to use it, all you need to do is add
table_type equals ICEBERG when you're creating
a new table in Athena using the Create Table command.
And this allows you, like I said,
to have concurrent users safely making
row level modifications or deletions, whatever it is,
without worrying about them stomping on each other.
This is actually compatible with Elastic Map Reduce,
Apache Spark and anything that supports
the Apache Iceberg table format.
The good thing is that it removes any need
for custom record locking.
So without ACID support, you would need to have some sort
of a solution for locking a record
and unlocking it surrounding any modifications to it
so that if two people were hitting the same record
at the same time and trying to write to it,
they wouldn't be fighting with each other.
Iceberg and ACID transactions
just does that for you automatically now.
Also a little side benefit
is that it gives you what's called time travel operations.
So you actually have the ability to recover data
that was recently deleted,
just using a plain old select statement.
So some of the historical data that is keeping around
for the purpose of ACID transactions
can be used for that purpose.
Now remember when we talked about governed tables
in Lake Formation?
Well, this is kind of another way of doing the same thing.
So governed tables gave us ACID support on S3 tables
in Lake Formation, but this is another way
of getting acid features with Athena.
So you could set up a governed table in Lake Formation
and then hit that table with Athena,
and you would have ACID support.
This is just another way of doing it.
So you can just create a table explicitly
from Athena directly with a table type of Iceberg,
and you'll get ACID support on that as well.
So kind of two different ways
of solving the same problem there.
Now, you might also remember that in Lake Formation
with governed tables, it had a feature
to automatically compact those tables over time,
because over time there's sort of this overhead
that builds up and it can actually make your performance
degrade as time goes on.
Now with Athena ACID, at least for now,
you do need to do that yourself periodically.
So if you are using acid transactions in Athena,
you'll probably wanna do a command like this
once in a while.
Optimize table, rewrite data using BIN_PACK
where a catalog equals whatever.
So a command like that will go back
and compact your data that's sort of been bloated
by this ACID support over time and make it performant again.
So that's the kind of thing
I could see showing up on the exams,
that kind of trivia.
What do you do if your ACID transactions
are getting slower over time?
Well, the answer would be
to periodically compact them using the BIN_PACK
command here that you're seeing.
That's Athena ACID in a nutshell.
An exciting new feature in 2022 as more
and more of the AWS data analytics world
goes to ACID support.

# 149. Apache Iceberg and Athena / EMR / Glue Integration
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/49075315
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: So you might have noticed
that I dropped Apache Iceberg
when I was talking about ACID support in Athena.
And you might say, wait, what's Apache Iceberg?
Maybe you're not familiar with that.
So brief primer, Apache Iceberg is a table format
for large scale data lakes,
and it is designed for big ones, petabyte-scale potentially.
Originally, this was created by Netflix
to solve their own data processing problems,
but they open-sourced it,
so anyone can use it now, including AWS.
The thing about Iceberg is that it offers ACID compliance,
and that means you can have transactional consistency
for any adds, removals, and modifications
to the files in your data lake.
So that could be an issue if you have a bunch
of producers and consumers on your data lake
that are kind of fighting with each other.
It can make sure that everything's consistent
and properly atomic during those operations.
Those row-level updates and deletes can also be important
for GDPR compliance specifically,
which is part of what's driving
Iceberg's popularity these days.
It also provides mechanisms for schema evolution,
to make it easier to change the schema of your data,
and change the format of your tables, and add new columns,
and delete them, whatever you need to do
safely as data evolves.
So previously, there might be issues where if you were
to restore a column that you deleted before,
it might have kind of like,
zombie data in there and stuff like that.
Iceberg makes sure stuff like that doesn't happen,
and it also makes it easy to do that just
through a query instead of something lower level.
It has partitioning features as well.
So again, just through a query,
you can change the partitioning of your underlying data.
It can support partition evolution,
change that over time if you need to,
update your partition schemes
as you need to as time goes on,
and also update your data volumes
over time as well very easily.
Also important, it supports time travel query.
So that means you can actually query your data
as it was at a specific point in time in the past,
and you can see how that might be useful.
You can use that to verify changes between updates,
or just go back and do a query based on
what things looked like at some given point in the past.
That might be useful.
It's also useful for doing easy rollback,
so if you need to roll your table back
to some point in time, the time travel capabilities
of Iceberg make that simple.
It also provides efficient metadata management,
kind of at a high level, that's what it does,
and it works with Spark, Flink,
Trino, Presto, and Hive.
And of course, Spark is something you can use
within the AWS ecosystem
within EMR or even SageMaker as well.
But more recently, it also is integrated directly
with AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, and Amazon Athena.
So that's what we talked about earlier,
how you can use Athena with Iceberg
to support ACID compliance.
So let's talk a little bit more about how that works.
By the way, this little screenshot on the right here
is from the create notebook UI for Amazon Athena.
And you can see that when you're creating a new notebook,
you can actually specify Apache Iceberg
as one of the table formats you can choose from.
So that's where you would see Iceberg
show up in the actual UI.
So how does this all fit together?
So, let's take a look at the diagram on the right here.
That kind of sums it up.
So basically, you can use AWS Glue as the place of Hive,
which is what Iceberg usually uses
as the source of its table metadata.
So up on top you have Spark, or Trino, or Flink,
or maybe even Athena, right?
And that goes through the Iceberg API,
which is just an API that Iceberg provides
for interacting with iceberg formatted tables.
And now, instead of Hive,
which is what we normally use by default,
we're gonna substitute in AWS's Glue catalog
as the metadata store.
And as we'll see, there are some
migration steps you need to do
to make that Glue catalog compatible with Iceberg,
but it can be done.
So Iceberg will communicate with your Glue catalog
for getting metadata about your data,
what the column names are, how it's laid out,
all that stuff, what the data types are,
and then it will also talk to Amazon S3
for the actual underlying data storage in your data lake.
So Iceberg's API is communicating
with Glue catalog for that metadata.
You'll retrieve and store data from Amazon S3,
and normally that will be in Parquet format
to be column-optimized and more efficient
for use with Iceberg.
And then Spark, or Flink, or whatever else
can sit on top of the Iceberg API
to do all of its stuff with ACID compliance.
So again, Athena can also be up there at the top now too,
and you can see how this is going to be using Iceberg
as a means for implementing ACID compliance from Athena.
So, with Athena sitting up there on top
instead of Spark or whatever,
you can see that it can just rely
on the Iceberg API for that ACID compliance,
and all the other features
that Iceberg gives you basically for free,
as long as you have an underlying Glue catalog
that's been migrated to be compatible with Iceberg.
So what does that look like?
So there's a few ways of doing that migration.
Glue data catalogs have to be made compatible
with the Iceberg API to be used with Iceberg.
So, it doesn't just happen out of the box.
But, once you've done that, Athena, and Spark,
and anything else can then use Iceberg as that intermediary
for asset transactions and everything else.
It can also give you compliance,
like we talked about, GDPR might need this sort of a thing.
It allows you to do things
like expiring old versions of tables,
and also have audit trails
that might be required by various regulations.
It can also give you historical reporting
with time travel queries,
and it can also solve a lot
of those consistency issues you might have
from many active producers and consumers
fighting with each other over the data in your data lake.
So, those are all good reasons to do this.
There's a couple of ways to go about it.
One is in-place migration.
In that approach, you leave your data where it is,
and you don't actually create a copy of it,
you just create new Iceberg metadata alone.
So you're only going to migrate the metadata
and not the underlying data store in that scenario.
Now, the downside of that is that it does not allow
for any schema or partition changes going forward.
So that is a trade off there.
However, it does mean you're not
gonna be duplicating your data in this process.
So if you have a large data lake
and you don't wanna pay for twice the storage,
in-place might be something to consider.
However, there's also a shadow migration you can do,
that approach will copy the data over,
and that allows you to do
additional validation along the way
and also have easier rollback and recovery as well.
And it also uncovers the full range of support
that Iceberg will give you.
A little example here on the right
of what you might actually type into the Athena Query editor
right in the UI to actually do
one of those shadow migrations.
And you can see it's actually pretty straightforward.
You would just create a new table
with a table type of Iceberg and a format of Parquet
in some S3 location that you're gonna create it in.
And you can then just say, hey,
select that from my source database
from wherever it's coming from,
and copy that over into
the required format that Iceberg wants.
So typically that's gonna be the way to go
if you can afford the extra data storage costs.

which can run a Spark application

So Apache Spark is an open source
distributed processing framework
commonly used for big data workloads.

it sits alongside MapReduce as sort of a replacement
for the analysis part of this stack.
So thanks to YARN,
we can swap out MapReduce for something better.
MapReduce was great 10 years ago,
but these days, Spark outperforms it by quite a bit.
And that's because Spark has in-memory caching.
It does most of its operations in memory
instead of hitting disc or going across the network.
And it also has a query execution optimizer.
So we can actually look at a complicated SQL query
and optimize that
to make sure that you have this really optimal
directed acyclic graph
that runs your query in the most efficient manner possible.
So it's not limited to the map and reduce paradigm.
It can do more complex operations more efficiently.
And it can really be orders of magnitude
faster than MapReduce as a result of that.
As a result, you really see Spark being used these days

Spark can be written using Java, Scala, Python, or R.

Spark itself is written in Scala by the way.

you can really reuse your code
across different applications.

everything, all these different modules
have a common interface.

You can use it for batch processing,

we mean information graphs,
you know, like a social network, that kind of a graph.

Now, Spark is not made for OLTP.
It's not built
for throwing thousands of transactions per second against it
from some, you know, forward,
you know, external facing website or something like that.
It's an OLAP thing.
It's meant for running longer lived queries
that might take a few seconds or minutes
or maybe even longer to complete.
So it's really for analysis for OLAP applications,
not for OLTP.
Remember that.
How does it work?
Well, here's what the Spark architecture looks like.
Spark applications are broken up into individual processes
that run across your cluster.
So at the heart of it all is a SparkContext
called your driver program.
This driver program coordinates all these other processes
through your cluster manager,
which might be Spark's own built-in cluster manager,
or in the case of EMR or a Hadoop cluster, YARN,
yet another resource negotiator,
the cluster manager that's built into Hadoop.
But you can run a standalone Spark cluster as well

And then we have the executors
that are doing all the grunt work.
So the executors run all the computations
and store the data associated with your job.
And remember, in EMR, that might be running on a core node
that has HDFS capability or a task node that does not.
The SparkContext is responsible
for sending application code to those executors
and sending individual tasks to those executors to complete.
Spark is made up of various components.
So at the root of it all is Spark Core.
This is the foundation of the platform.
It's responsible for memory management,
fault recovery, scheduling,
distributing and monitoring jobs,
interacting with your storage system,
which might be HDFS or EMRFS or something else,
and it also supports all the guts needed
to talk to Java, Scala, Python, or our scripts.
Under the hood at this low level,
it uses something called
the resilient distributed dataset, or RDD,
but probably don't need to know that for the exam.
On top of Spark Core are four main systems,
one is Spark SQL,
and this has evolved
into really a fundamental piece of Spark these days.
Spark SQL is a distributed query engine
that provides low latency interactive queries
up to 100 times faster than MapReduce.
And it can support various data sources and formats
like JDBC, ODBC, JSON, HDFS, Orc, Parquet, or HiveQL
if you're gonna be querying Hive tables.
But the important thing about Spark SQL
is that it introduces what's called a dataset object,
or in the world of Python, a data frame.
And basically, this allows you to treat your data in Spark

and query it just like it were one.
So that's really the power of Spark SQL.
It kind of gives us this SQL style interface
to our underlying data on the EMR cluster.
We also have Spark Streaming.
Spark Streaming is a realtime solution

MLLib, very important feature there.

Let's talk a little bit more about Spark Streaming

So Spark applications

so pretty much everything talks SQL these days.

You query it in the same way

the CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statement or CTAS for short.

in the context of Amazon Athena,

The syntax might be a little bit different though.
Very similar in spirit
to a materialized view in Redshift,
it creates a new table from query results.
So you can do any SELECT statement you can imagine,
and create a new table from the result of that query.
And maybe you can use that to create a new table
that's a subset of another table.

from this old table for some subset
of what's in that table and create a new table
based on that query result."
However, it's also a neat little trick
for converting data into a new underlying format.
And this is especially interesting remembering
that Athena can sit on top of a data lake in S3.
So you could use this as a way to convert data in S3
to a totally different format
that might be more performant for Athena, right?
So for example, let's take a look
at these two examples down below here.
The one on the left we're saying
CREATE TABLE new table WITH format equals Parquet,
write compression equals SNAPPY
AS SELECT star FROM old table.
So what's going on here?
We're gonna select everything from old table,
and we're just gonna rewrite it into a table
called a new table.
But along the way, we're gonna change it to Parquet,
which is a columnar format that's gonna be better optimized
for doing queries in Athena,
and also with SNAPPY compression
to further optimize it as well.
So this is a little easy way to very quickly compress,
or change the format of your raw data in S3,
and change it into something that works much more
efficiently with Athena.
Another example on the right here, we're same spirit here,
we're selecting everything from old table,
and putting it into a new table called my orc ctas table.
In this case, not only are we changing the format
to ORC along the way,
we're also specifying a new external location.
So I'm saying,
"Okay, not only do I want to change the format
for this table, I'm gonna explicitly store it
within this S3 path within my Athena results bucket."
Right?
So that's kind of an finishing trick,
'cause not only are we changing how it's exposed
to Athena itself, we were also changing,
and storing the underlying raw data
into this other table in S3.
So that might be a quick and dirty way
of doing data transformations or transforming
the actual format of the underlying data,
the raw data into something else just using Athena.
And then I can go to that S3 bucket,
and pick it up there if I want to.

# 161. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305578
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: So the first service you need to know about
is Kinesis Data Streams.
And Kinesis Data Streams is a way for you
to stream big data in your systems.
So a Kinesis Data Stream is made of multiple shards,
and shards are numbered, number one, number two,
all the way to number N.
And this is something you have to provision ahead of time.
So when you start with Kinesis Data Streams, you're saying,
"Hey, I want a stream with six shards."
And so the data is going to be split
across all the shards, okay?
And the shards are going to be defining your stream capacity
in terms of ingestion and consumption rates.
So for now, let's just start with this.
And then we have producers.
So producers send data into Kinesis Data Streams.
And producers can be manyfold, they could be applications,
they could be clients such as desktop or mobile clients,
they could be leveraging the AWS SDK
at a very, very low level,
or the Kinesis Producer Library KPL at a higher level,
and we'll have a deeper dive on to the producers
in the next lectures.
Or it could be the Kinesis Agent inside on the server
to stream, for example, application logs
into Kinesis Data Streams.
So all these producers do the exact same thing,
they rely on the SDK at a very, very low level,
and they're going to produce records
into our Kinesis Data Stream.
So a record at its fundamental is made of two things.
It's made of a partition key
and it is made of the data blob or the value
that is up to one megabytes.
So the partition key will define and help determine
in which shard will the record go to.
And the data blob is the value itself.
So when you have the producers sending data
to Kinesis Data Streams, they can send data
at a rate of one megabytes per second,
or a thousand messages per second per shard.
So if you have six shards, you get six megabytes per second,
or 6,000 messages per second overall, okay?
Now, once the data is in Kinesis Data Streams,
it can be consumed by many consumers.
And these consumers, again, can have many forms
and we'll explore them in detail in this section.
So we have applications and they could be relying on the SDK
or at a high level, the Kinesis Client Library, so KCL.
They could be Lambda functions
if you want to do serverless processing
on top of Kinesis Data Streams.
It could be Kinesis Data Firehose
as we'll see in this section,
or Kinesis Data Analytics.
So when the consumer receives the record,
he receives again, the partition key,
also a sequence number, which represents
where the record was in the shard,
as well as the data blob, so the data itself.
Now, we have different consumption modes
for Kinesis Data Streams.
We have two megabytes per second of throughput shared
for all the consumers per shard, okay?
Or you get two megabytes per second per shard, per consumer
if you are enabling the enhanced consumer mode,
the enhanced fan-out.
So we will look at it again
in the section in greater detail.
So again, producers send data to Kinesis Data Streams,
it stays in there for a while,
and then it is read by many different consumers.
Okay, some properties of Kinesis Data Streams.
The first one is that retention can be set
between 1 day to 365 days.
And that means that by default,
you have the ability to reprocess or replay data.
And once that data is inserted into Kinesis,
it cannot be deleted, that's called immutability.
Also, when you send messages to Kinesis Data Streams,
you add a partition key.
And messages that share the same partition key
will go to the same shard,
and that gives you key-based ordering.
For producers, you can send data using the SDK,
Kinesis Producer Library KPL, or the Kinesis Agent.
And for consumers, you can write your own.
So Kinesis Client Library, KCL, or the SDK,
or you can use a managed consumer on AWS,
such as AWS Lambda, Kinesis Data Firehose,
or Kinesis Data Analytics.
Now for capacity modes,
you have two options for Kinesis Data Streams.
The first one, that's the historic capacity mode,
it's called provisioned mode.
So you choose a number of shards provisioned
and then you can scale them manually or using an API.
And each shard in Kinesis Data Streams
is going to get one megabyte per second,
or 1000 records per second.
And then for the out throughput,
each shard will get two megabytes per second,
and this is applicable to classic or fan-out consumer.
You also pay per shard provisioned per hour,
so you need to think a lot in advance,
and that's why it's called provisioned mode.
But the second mode is a mirror mode called on-demand mode.
And in this, you don't need to provision
or manage the capacity.
That means that the capacity
will be adjusted over time on-demand.
You get the default capacity provision,
which is four megabytes per second
or 4,000 records per second.
And then there will be automatic scaling
based on the observed throughput peak
during the last 30 days.
And in this mode, you're still going to pay
per stream per hour, and per data in/out per gigabyte.
So a different pricing model.
So if you don't know your capacity and events,
go for on-demand,
but if you can plan capacity and events,
you should go for provisioned mode.
In terms of security for Kinesis Data Streams,
it is deployed within a region,
and so you have your shards.
You can control access to produce and read
from the shard using IAM policies.
There is encryption in flight using HTTPS,
and encryption at rest using KMS.
You can implement your own encryption and decryption
of data on the client-side,
which is called client-side encryption.
And it is harder to implement because you need
to encrypt the data yourself and decrypt it yourself,
but this enhances security.
VPC endpoints are available for Kinesis,
this allows you to access Kinesis directly
from an EC2 instance in a private subnet
without going through the internet.
And finally, all the API calls can be monitored
using CloudTrail.
So that's it for an overview of Kinesis Data Streams.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture for a deeper dive
on all the moving parts in Kinesis Data Streams.

# 165. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams - Enhanced Fan Out
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305628
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: So I'd like to make sure
I teach you about real world big data,
and not just exam big data,
and even though this might not be on exam just yet,
I think it will appear very soon.
And to me, Kinesis Enhanced Fan Out
is what I call a game-changing feature,
and it was appearing in August, 2018,
so I'm sure it will be on the exam very, very soon anyway.
So how do we leverage this?
Well, it will work if you use KCL 2.0
or AWS Lambda from November, 2018.
So it's supported by both these things.
And what does Enhanced Fan Out mean?
That means that each consumer
will get two megabytes per second, per shard.
So it looks similar as before,
but it's not exactly the same, right?
So we have a producer producing
to a Kinesis Data Streams
and has, for example, one shard in this example.
We'll have a consumer application A,
and it will do an API called SubscribeToShard,
and, automatically, Kinesis Data Streams
will start pushing data at the rate
of two megabytes per second.
So we're not pulling anymore.
We're just saying SubscribeToShard,
and the shard will send us two megabytes per second.
That means that if we have 20 consumers,
overall, we'll get 40 megabytes per second per shard.
So we can start adding on consumer application,
do the subscribe call again
and get another two megabytes per second.
So before, we had a two megabytes per second limit
per shard, but now we get two megabytes per second
per limit, per shard, per consumer.
The reason is because Enhanced Fan Out
has Kinesis pushing data to consumers over HTTP/2.
And the added benefit of this is, first of all,
we can scale a lot more consumer applications.
And the other one is we get a reduced latency.
So before, remember, we had this 200 milliseconds latency
in case we had one consumer
because it could pull five times a second,
and you actually, if you had more consumers,
they all had one second latency.
Well, with the Enhanced Fan Out,
now we get a reduced latency because data is pushed to us,
and on average you'll get 70 millisecond latency,
which is a lot less than 200 millisecond or one second.
So Enhanced Fan Out is to me a game changing feature,
and I'm just happy to tell you that it exists.
Obviously, you have to pay for it a bit more,
and the pricing page on AWS will help you understand
how much you have to pay for.
Now, what's the difference between Enhanced Fan Out
and consumer standards,
and when would you use each of those?
So a standard consumer,
you will use it when you have a low number
of consuming applications, say one, two, or three,
and you can tolerate some latency,
you can tolerate 200 milliseconds or more latency.
And you want to minimize cost because this cost
of standard consumer is included in Kinesis already.
And you will use Enhanced Fan Out Consumers
if you want to have multiple applications
consuming the same stream.
We're talking about like five
or 10 applications at the same time.
And you want very low latency requirements.
So you can only maybe tolerate
70 millisecond latency requirements.
And obviously, this will bring you a higher cost.
As I said, see the Kinesis pricing page for that.
And by default though, when you use Fan Out Consumer,
you have a limit of 20 consumers that can use Fan Out,
but you can increase that doing a service request
on AWS support.
So I hope that makes sense.
I hope you're excited about this new feature.
Honestly, it's awesome, and I'm pretty sure the exam
will ask you about it very, very soon.
So it's good to learn about it.
To me, it's game-changing
because now we can have 20 consumers on a shard
and not have any impact to each of them,
which to me is really, really game-changing.
All right, I've said it enough.
I will see you in the next lecture.

# 166. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams - Scaling
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305630
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: From an exam and real world perspective,
it's really important to understand
how you can scale Kinesis.
So the first operation you can do is to add shards
and adding shard in Kinesis world is called shard splitting,
and we'll see why in a second.
It can be used to basically increase the Stream capacity.
So remember how you get one megabyte per second
of data per shard,
then if you have 10 shards, you have 10 megabytes, right?
So if you want to increase the Stream capacity,
you need to split a shard.
It can also be helped to use and divide a hot shard.
So if you have a hot shard,
one shard that's being used more than others,
we'll just split it,
and it will probably increase our throughputs.
So what happens when you split a shard?
Well, the old shard is closed and will be deleted
once the data in it is expired.
So let's have a look with the diagram,
'cause I think it'll make a lot more sense.
So we have shard one, two, and three in this example,
and they occupy the same space.
Now shard two is very hot,
and we want to split it to increase throughput
on this key space of shard two.
So we're going to do a split operation,
and what's going to happen is
that there's gonna be shard four that's being created
and shard five that are being created.
And as you can see,
they're occupying the same space as shard two.
But now because we have two shards,
we have two megabyte per second on this space
instead of one megabyte per second.
Then the other shard, one and three, they remain the same.
So before our shard looks like this, it has three shards.
Our Stream looks like this, has three shards,
and then after the splits,
we have four shards,
and we can see that four and five
are occupying the space of shard two.
So shard two will be available
as long as the data in it is not expired,
but when it's expired, it will be gone.
So now this is the state of our new Kinesis Stream.
When producers write data to it,
they have four shards to write to.
So this is really important concept you understand
because basically you can split as many shards
as you want over time
and increase your throughput this way.
Now, what's the inverse operation
to adding or splitting shard?
Well, it's to decrease shard or merging shards.
And so when you merge shards,
you would use that to decrease the Stream capacity
and save on some cost.
And it can be used, for example,
to group two shards that have low traffic,
and you want to merge 'em together in order to save cost.
So the old shards will be closed and deleted again
based on data expiration.
So now, for example, say we have this shard, and it has,
our Stream, it has one, four and five,
three, just like before,
and we want to merge one and four together.
So we're going to merge them together,
and it's becoming shard six.
That's because maybe shard one and four
didn't get much traffic,
so we can merge them together and save some cost.
So we merge them together, and then shard five and three,
while they remain on the same as before,
and so now we've went from four shards
to three shards in our new Stream because we've merged it.
So you can see now how we can
merge and split and merge and split,
and we can basically modularize
our entire Kinesis data Stream
to increase and decrease throughputs over time.
This is how it works.
A common scenario question in the exam
will be asking you about a case
where the producer is sending data to a Kinesis Stream
with the correct partition key,
yet your consumer receive the data
out of order at some point.
And so a reason for that would be resharding,
so let's explore this use case.
So when you do a Kinesis resharding,
you can read straight from the child's shards
after the resharding.
However, if you haven't read all the data yet
from the parent shard,
then what's going to happen is
that you may read the data out of order
for a particular hash key.
So let's look at it in the diagram.
So we have the parent shard,
and we have a device producing to the Kinesis Stream,
using the KPL for example.
And we have a consumer application running on EC2,
using the SDK.
So we're going to do get records, API calls.
So say that the IoT device
just before a resharding operation
sends some data, one and two.
So in terms of consumption rates,
our consumer application has been consuming
everything in the parent shard
up to the two data points, one and two.
Then we start a shard splitting operation.
So from this parent shard,
we're going to have two new child shards.
And what's going to happen is that once the split is over,
well the IoT device is going to start producing
to the new children shard
because the parent shard will be closed for rights.
So that means that the data points three and four
are going to end up on the child shard.
Now if your consumer application isn't very, very smart,
what's going to happen is that you can request data
directly from the child shard
before you have read the end of the parent.
So that means that you will see data points
three and four first and then maybe one and two next.
So this is something that can create out of records order,
out of order records, sorry, after a resharding operation.
So the guideline is that
after a reshard in your consumer application logic,
you need to make sure that you have the logic
to read entirely from the parent
until there are no new records from the parent.
That means you reached the end of the parent shard,
and then you can start reading from the child shard,
and this will guarantee the order of the records.
Now this can be complicated to implement, so as a note,
the Kinesis Client Library, the KCL,
already has this logic built in
even after the resharding operation,
so you're good to go.
But hopefully, you're good with that use case,

So what about Auto Scaling, you may say,
do we have to do this thing manually?
Well, there is Auto Scaling,

So what about Kinesis Scaling?
What are the limitations of it?
Well, you cannot do resharding in parallel,

So that means you can't like reshard 1,000 Streams at a time

And you can only perform one resharding operation at a time.
It takes a few seconds.
So for example, if you have 1,000 shards,

It takes time.

On top of it, there are some limitations.
