# 167. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams - Handling Duplicates
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305636
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Now, let's talk about
how you can handle duplicate records
in Kinesis data streams.
And there are two cases when that can happen.
There is on the producer side and also on the consumer side.
So Producer retries can create duplicates
due to mainly network timeouts.
And this is an exam question.
So how does that work?
Well you have your producers, it could be applications,
it could be using like SDK or the KPL,
and they're producing into a Kinesis data stream.
Now, when we do a PutRecord and we send some data,
then we know what happens.
The data gets written into the Kinesis data stream.
The data gets a unique sequence number.
And then can you see the stream says,
I've written your data correctly,
but in case of a network timeout,
then this acknowledgement
may never reach our producer application,
maybe due to a network timeout.
And our producer cannot know that.
So maybe it says,
okay I don't think this record has been written
because I haven't received any acknowledgement back,
and now there's a timeout.
So what's going to happen is that
the producer record is going to be retried
by our application by reissuing an API call.
So we're going to do a PutRecord again for the same data,
which is going to be written a second time
into my data stream.
And as you can see,
the sequence number has increased from 123 to 124,
and now the acknowledgement reaches back to our producer
and we are good to go.
But what happened is that,
from a Kinesis data stream perspective,
we have created duplicate records
because the same data was written twice
and it got two different sequence ID.
So although the two records have identical data,
they also have unique sequence numbers.
And so there will be two data points
in our Kinesis data stream.
So the fix for it is to embed a unique record ID in the data
to be able to deduplicate based on
that unique record ID on the consumer side.
So this, although it looks scary,
I would say rarely happens,
but still is a case for you to know about
and something the exam will test you on.
Now let's talk about what can happen on
the consumer side for duplicates.
So the consumer retries
can make your application read the same data twice
and the consumer retries can happen
in four different type of use cases,
but they all correspond
to when your record processor will restart.
So it could be when a worker terminates unexpectedly.
It could be when a worker instances are added or removed.
It could be when shards are merged or split
or when the application is deployed.
So remember these four cases,
'cause they can come up as well in the exam.
So the fix for that is quite difficult
and the documentation is pretty vague about it.
But the idea is that
you make your consumer application idempotent.
That means that if you read the same data twice,
then it does not have twice the same side effects.
And the other recommendation provided by the documentation
in AWS is that if somehow your final destination
can handle duplicates, it's recommended to do it there.
For example, if you can rely on that unique record ID
and you insert that into a database,
then the database will not allow you to insert
that unique record ID twice.
And so that could be a good one for you.
If you want more information,
you can read the documentation here.
But from an exam perspective,
you need to know that network timeouts
can introduce producer-side duplicates
and that these four consumer retries
can introduce duplicates from a consumer perspective
because the data is going to be read twice.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 169. Amazon Data Firehose
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305642
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so we've seen Kinesis Data Streams.
Now, Firehose.
So, Firehose is actually quite easy.
It is to store data into target destinations.
So we have producers and it could be, again,
a bunch of applications from before
that can send directly the data into Kinesis Data Firehose,
or Kinesis Data Firehose can read
from your Kinesis Data Streams,
from Amazon CloudWatch or AWS IoT.
But the most common you're going to see
is going to be Firehose reading from Kinesis Data Streams.
So it's going to read the records one by one,
up to one megabyte at a time, okay?
And then if you want to transform the record,
we could have a Lambda function
created to transform the record
to do some small modification.
And then, Kinesis Data Firehose
will try to fill a big batch of data
to write that data into a target database
or a target destination, okay?
So that's why it's called batch writes.
It doesn't write stuff instantaneously.
It will try to batch them to write them efficiently.
So therefore, Kinesis Data Firehose
is a near real time service.
So in terms of destinations, we have AWS.
So Amazon S3 is very important.
Amazon Redshift, and to write to Redshift,
Kinesis Data Firehose will first write into Amazon S3,
and then issue a copy command into Redshift
or Amazon OpenSearch.
And you have to remember these three destinations,
they're very important.
Other destinations include
third-party destinations from partners
such as Datadog, Splunk, New Relic, and MongoDB,
but they could be others coming up in the future.
You don't need to know them.
So this is why we'll not update this slide
if there are new partners,
but you can see that there will be new partners over time,
or also there could be a custom destination.
As long as there is a valid HTTP endpoint as an API,
you can have Firehose deliver data into that destination.
And finally, if you have failure for processing

# 170. Kinesis Data Stream Troubleshooting and Performance Tuning
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40394454
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: These exams love to give you scenarios
of when things go wrong and how to fix them.
So let's spend a little bit of time
talking about troubleshooting steps
for various Kinesis data stream issues you might run into.
Let's start with the performance on the producer end.
So let's say that we have writes being too slow
from my data stream producer.
There's a few causes of that.
One might be that you're encountering service limits.
You might just wanna check for throughput exceptions
to see if that's what's happening.
If so, the exceptions might point you toward
what the problem is.
So different calls have different limits
and you might just be exceeding those limits.
There are also shard level limits for reads
and writes that you might be exceeding.
We talked about those earlier,
and some operations have stream level limits as well.
So for CreateStream, ListStreams and DescribeStreams
at the stream level, the rate limits on that
are anywhere between five and 20 calls per second.
Also, you might be counting hot shards, you know, data skew.
We talked about that way back in the first section.
So maybe that's what's going on.
Maybe you need a better partition key
to better evenly distribute your puts across the shards.
Maybe you have a hot shard that's slowing
things down when you're producing.
If you have a large producer,
it can help to batch things up.
So you can use the Kinesis Producer Library
with the PutRecords API
to batch up multiple records together
and send them all together at once.
That can be a lot more efficient.
Or maybe aggregate your records into larger files
and then send those larger files across
instead of individual records.
Smaller producers like an app,
same advice applies with PutRecords.
You can also use something called Kinesis Recorder
in the AWS Mobile SDKs to do that automatically.
Some other issues you might see with producers,
if you're getting 500 or 503 errors back,
that usually indicates that you're seeing
Amazon Kinesis exceptions more than 1% of the time.
The way to deal with that is to implement a retry mechanism
so that you don't just fail,
you try it again until it works.
You might be seeing connection errors from Flink to Kinesis.
If so, that could point to a network issue
or not enough resources in the Flink environment,
or could also be a VPC misconfiguration.
Maybe you just can't get from Flink to Kinesis
because they're in different VPC subnets
or you're not using VPC peering.
If you're seeing timeout errors from Flink to Kinesis,
connections are okay, but timeouts are happening.
Well, you can just increase the timeout
with the RequestTimeout setting.
You can also set a higher queue limit
on the Flink Kinesis producer.
And you might be seeing throttling errors coming in.
If so, check for hot shards again,
using enhanced monitoring at the shard-level
to see what's going on.
You can also check your logs for what's called micro spikes,
where you're seeing these sudden bursts of traffic
that you can't handle, or you might be seeing obscure
metrics that are breaching their limits
that can point to those sorts of micro spikes.
You can also try a different partitioning strategy,
try a random partition key,
or just try to improve the keys distribution.
Again, it could be hot shards and if you do have data skew
going on, a different partition key
is a way to try to address that.
You can also implement an exponential backoff mechanism,
so if you are hitting throttling limits,
then you can have a system
that automatically backs off on the producer's side
until things get caught up.
And you can just do old school rate limiting as well.
Make sure that you're never sending more than a given rate
that's more than you can handle.
Let's also look at the consumer side
and some issues you might see on the consumer end.
If I'm seeing records getting skipped
with Kinesis Client Library, that might mean I need to check
for unhandled exceptions on process records.
If I'm seeing records in the same shard
process by more than one processor,
that might indicate that failover is happening
on the record processor workers
and I might need to adjust that fail over time.
One way of dealing with that as well is to handle
shutdown methods that come in with a reason "Zombie,"
that is what happens when you're seeing things
being processed by more than one thing.
If my reads are just too slow,
I can increase the number of shards.
That's kind of the basic thing to do.
Or it might be that my max records per call is too low.
It could also just be that your code is too slow.
So to see if your code on the consumer side
is the bottleneck, just test an empty processor
versus your own and see if that performs better.
GetRecords might be returning empty results for you
on the consumer side, it turns out that's totally normal.
Just keep calling GetRecords.
There are situations where data just won't be ready
yet, so don't worry about that.
If your shard iterator is expiring unexpectedly,
that might indicate that you need more write capacity
on the shard table in DynamoDB under the hood.
And finally, if record processing is falling behind,
one way to buy some time is to increase the retention period
while you're trying to figure out the real issue.
But usually that points to a problem
with insufficient resources.
So monitor that using
the GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds metric,
and the MillisBehindLatest metric
while you're trying to figure out
what that resource limitation might be.
Some other issues on the consumer side,
maybe your Lambda function isn't getting invoked.
That's usually a permissions issue on the execution role.
So go check your IAM permissions on the Lambda function
to make sure Kinesis can talk to it.
Your function might also be timing out,
so check the max execution time on that Lambda function.
Make sure it's large enough to handle what you need to do.
You could be breaching the concurrency limits
on your Lambda function
and keep an eye on the Iterator age metric
to see whether the Lambda's getting backed up or not.
You might also be seeing ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded
exceptions coming in on the consumer side.
That indicates that throttling is happening.
You might need to re shard your stream in response to that
or reduce the size of the GetRecords requests.
This is also a situation where enhanced fan-out can help,
so that might make for a good exam question.
I'm seeing ReadProvisionThroughputExceeded exceptions.
What might be a way of dealing with that?
One of those answers might be use enhanced fan-out.
You can also use retries and exponential back off
to try to settle at a better throughput rate
that you can handle.
A few more here.
If you're seeing high latency on the consumer side,
you can monitor that with GetRecords.Latency
and IteratorAge while you're trying to figure out
what's going on and troubleshoot it.
But the first thing to try
is just increasing the number of shards.
You might not have enough and also increase
the retention period to make sure things don't get dropped.
Check the CPU and memory utilization.
You might need more memory to handle things more quickly.
Again, if you're seeing 500 errors,
that's the same thing as on the producer side.
It indicates you're getting a high exception rate
of more than 1%.
All you can do there is make sure
that you have a retry mechanism
so that if you're getting an exception,
you're trying again instead of just getting a 500.
And you can see a blocked or stuck KCL application
on the consumer side.
If so, you might need to optimize
your process records method and make it faster.
You might need to increase your max leases per worker,
or you might need to enable KCL debug logs
to see what's going on in more depth
and figure out what the underlying issue really is.

# 172. Kinesis Analytics Costs; RANDOM_CUT_FOREST
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40356564
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk about Kinesis Analytics cost model.
It is serverless.
So you just pay for the resources you consume and nothing else.
It scales up for you automatically, and you don't have to worry about the underlying resources needed
to actually run your Kinesis Analytics applications.
However, it's not cheap, unlike some other serverless services that AWS offers.
When I was making this course, Kinesis Analytics actually made up the bulk of the actual charges that
I incurred while developing this course.
So use it carefully and do make sure to shut down any analytics jobs once you're done using them.
Just to be safe.
As far as security goes, you can use IAM permissions to access the streaming, source and destination
services that you're working with, so you can configure IAM to allow your Kinesis Analytics application
to talk to whatever upstream and downstream services it needs to communicate to.
There's also a cool feature in Kinesis Analytics called Schema Discovery, and that's how the column
names in your SQL are found.
It can actually analyze the incoming data from your stream as you're setting it up.
So you can check that it worked, but it's pretty cool.
It can actually analyze an incoming stream and write in the AWS console.
You can see how it's trying to make sense of that data and impart a schema on top of it, and you can
edit and correct that data as needed.
It's also worth talking about something called random cut forest.
This is a SQL function offered by Kinesis Data Analytics that you can use within your data analytics
application for anomaly detection on any numeric columns in a stream.
And you can tell that AWS is really proud of this because they published a whole paper on it, and you
can go look it up if you want to.
It is a novel way of identifying outliers in a data set so you can handle them however you need to.
An example of doing this that they give in the paper is detecting anomalous subway ridership during
the New York City Marathon.
So they have a stream of data of people going through the subway turnstiles, and they are using random
cut forest to automatically identify anomalies in that rate of usage of the subway system.
So this is important because if you ever see a question about trying to detect anomalies or outliers
in a stream of data, random cut forest with Kinesis Analytics is very likely a good answer for that.

# 180. Amazon OpenSearch Service Performance
# Section: Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40356608
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: A few quick notes on optimizing performance
of your Amazon OpenSearch cluster.
One thing to think about is memory pressure in the JVM, and a couple
of scenarios that can result in that
are having unbalanced shard allocations across your nodes.
So if you have a certain set of
shards that are doing most of the work and
a few that are just sitting there doing nothing,
that can cause memory pressure on the overworked shards.
And when you run out of memory,
bad things happen, right?
You start swapping memory to disc in your performance tanks.
So often, that can result in performance issues.
Also, having too many shards in a cluster
can also cause trouble.
Sort of a fundamental truth of distributed computing
is that less can be more sometimes.
The act of distributing that processing
often takes more work than you think
and specifically can take a lot of memory to manage it all.
So the takeaway from all
this is that if you're seeing JVM memory pressure
errors in your logs, often you can fix that by having fewer shards
to yield better performance.
And the way to get fewer shards is by deleting older,
unused indices if you can.
So if there's a way to offload data from your cluster
into some archive where you don't need it as much,
maybe you can unload data off the glacier or
something and delete the indices associated
with that old, unused data, that
might be a good way to get around that
JVM memory pressure error.
Or maybe you have indices that just aren't used at all.
Get rid of them. That'll help too.
So yeah, just a quick
note here on avoiding the JVM memory pressure error specifically
within Amazon OpenSearch.

it can be consumed many times by different applications.

and this is the feature
that allows the data to be consumed many times.

it is preserved at a shard level,
even during replays,

It's also possible for you
to build multiple applications reading
from the same stream independently,

a big data frameworks, such as Spark or Flink,

For SQS, it's very different.

There is a replay capability for Kinesis Data Streams,
whereas there is no replay capability for the others.
The maximum data retention is 365 days
for Kinesis Data Streams,
zero days for can see Kinesis Data Firehose,
so the data is just sent to the destination and forgotten.
And for SQS standard and SQS FIFO,
it is 14 days.
In terms of scaling and throughputs,
we have two provision shards
for Kinesis Data Streams in the provisioned mode.
So we get one megabytes per second per producer per shard,
or two megabytes per second per consumer per shard.
And for the on-demand mode,
then you have as much scaling as you want,
and you don't need to choose
the number of shards ahead of time.
No scaling limits for Kinesis Data Firehose
and SQS Standard.
And for SQS FIFO,
you have 3,000 message per second with batching,
or 30,000 messages per second with batching,
if you use the high throughput mode for SQS FIFO.
In terms of object size,
the max object size is one megabytes
for Kinesis Data Streams.
128 megabytes at destination for Kinesis Data Firehose,
one megabyte for SQS,
but you can extend it if you use the Extend Library
to store the messages outside of SQS
and only send some metadata in SQS.
So I think now we know they're very different.
For the use cases of SQS,
you have order processing, image processing,
or auto-scaling queues according to messages
or to buffer and batch messages for future processing
or to offload a request from one service to another.
Whereas Kinesis Data Streams have different use cases,
for example, fast log
and event data collection and processing,
real-time metrics and reports,
mobile data capture, real-time data analytics,
gaming data feed,
complex stream processing,
data feed from Internet of Things.
Okay, so, hopefully, now you understand
the differences between the two.
You're very confident in it
and I hope you liked this lecture.

# 188. Amazon SQS - Dead Letter Queues
# Section: Application Integration
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305784
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Now, let's talk about
dead letter queues in SQS.
The idea is that let's get into this scenario
where a consumer fails to process a message
within the visibility timeout period.
Then we know that the message
automatically goes back into the queue.
So the consumer reads the message, maybe there's a failure,
maybe we don't have enough time,
the message goes back into the queue.
Now, if that thing happens very often,
that can be a problem.
For example, we read again the message,
maybe there's something wrong with the message.
Maybe our consumer doesn't understand the message
or can't process the message.
Then the message will go back into the queue.
And it will happen again.
We'll read the message again from SQS,
and it will go again back into the queue.
So we can set a threshold to how many times this can happen.
And this failure loop can be a big problem,
but we can set a MaximumReceives threshold.
And if that threshold is exceeded, then we can tell SQS
to say, well, this message looks a bit odd.
It looks like it's being processed too many times
and not successfully.
Therefore, send this into a dead letter queue.
And the dead letter queue will contain that message
and for later processing, and so the message will be removed
from the first queue and sent into the second one.
Why do we have dead letter queues?
Well, dead letter queues are very useful for debugging.
And in case a message goes in dead letter queue,
because it is an SQS queue, you have to process it,
but at least it gives you time
to understand what is happening.
A few things to notice that the dead letter queue
of a FIFO queue must also be a FIFO queue,
and the dead letter queue of the standard queue
must also be a standard queue.
Finally, because we have a dead letter queue,
you need to make sure that the messages
are processed before they expire from the queue.
So it's a good idea to set a long time, for example,
14 days of retention from within the dead letter queue.
And the next feature for management
of your dead letter queues
are the redrive to source feature.
So it's a feature to help you consume messages
in the dead letter queue
to understand what is wrong with them.
So you have your messages now,
you know they haven't been processed in the source queue
and therefore, they are in the dead letter queue.
And you're going to do a manual inspection
and debugging of these messages.
And then you're going to fix your consumer code,
understand why the message wasn't processed,
in case the message was correct.
And then what you can do is, redrive that message
from the dead letter queue into the source SQS queue.
And what's going to happen with this
is that the consumer can now reprocess
that message without even knowing
that the message went into the dead letter queue,
and then the message processing has happened.
And that's a cool feature.
So now, let's go into the console
so I can show you the dead letter queue feature.

# 191. Amazon SNS - with SQS Fan Out
# Section: Application Integration
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40305830
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Now let's talk about
the SNS + SQS fan out pattern.
The idea is that you want a message
to be sent to multiple SQS queues,
but if you send them individually to every SQS queue,
there can be problems associated with it.
For example, if your application crashes in between,
if there are delivery failures,
or if you add more SQS queues down the road.
Therefore we want to use the fan out pattern.
The idea is that you're going to push once in SNS topic
and then you're going to subscribe
as many SQS queues as you want to the SNS topic.
These queues are subscribers,
and they will all receive the messages sent into SNS.
So for example, we have a buying service that wants
to send messages into two SQS queues.
What it will do instead, it will send one message
into an SNS topic, and the queues are subscribers
of that SNS topic so that the fraud service
and the shipping service can read all messages
from their own SQS queues.
The idea with this as well is that it's
a fully decoupled model, and there is no data loss.
SQS will give you data persistence, delayed processing,
as well as retries of work, and with this pattern,
we can add more SQS queues as a subscriber
of the SNS topic over time.
For this, we need to make sure
that you SQS queue access policy, as we've seen from before,
allows your SNS topic to write to your SQS queue.
So again, yet another use case
for using queue access policies.
And we have cross region delivery.
So it's definitely possible for an SNS topic
in one region to send messages to SQS queues
in other regions if the security allows it.
Next, so how do we use this pattern for other purposes,
for example, S3 events into multiple queues?
So there is a limitation of S3 event rules is that
for a combination of event type, for example,
an object is being created and a prefix, for example,
images/ you can only have one S3 event rule.
But what if you want to send the same S3 event notification
to multiple SQS queues?
In that case, you would use the fan out pattern.
So for example, we have S3 object created
as an event appearing in your S3 bucket,
and we will send this event into an SNS topic,
and we will subscribe many SQS queues
to the SNS topic as a final pattern.
But we could also subscribe other type of application,
email, Lambda functions, et cetera, et cetera.
And then what we get from this is that the message
of the event happening in Amazon S3 is going to go
to many different destinations thanks
to this fan out pattern.
Another architecture is that you can send data directly
from SNS to Amazon S3 through Kinesis Data Firehose.
So because SNS has a direct integration with KDF,
then your buying service can send data into an SNS topic.
Then can you see Data Fire Host KDF will
receive that information,
and then from Kinesis Data Firehose,
you can send it into your Amazon S3 bucket,
or for that matter, any supported KDF specific destination,
which allows you to be really extensible
in the way you want to maybe persist
your messages from your SNS topic.
So we can apply the final pattern to FIFO topics as well.
So Amazon SNS has a FIFO or FIFO capability,
which is first in first out,
which gives ordering of messages in the topic.
So the producers send the messages one, two, three, four.
And the subscribers can only be an SQS FIFO queue for now,
which is receiving messages one, two, three, four in order.
So the idea is that with SNS FIFO, we get the same features
as SQS FIFO, we get ordering by message group ID.
We get deduplication using a deduplication ID
or content-based deduplication, and both SQS standard
and FIFO queues can be subscribers.
In terms of throughputs, you're limited.
You get the same throughputs as the SQS FIFO queue,
because right now only SQS FIFO queues can read
from SNS FIFO topics.
So why do we need this?
Well, in case you wanna do a fan out using SQS FIFO.
So you need fan out, ordering, and deduplication.
So the buying service will send the data
into an SNS FIFO topic, and then it will fan out
to two SQS FIFO queue, which can have the fraud service
and the shipping service read from FIFO queues as well.
One last feature of SNS that can be really handy
regarding the fan out pattern is
that you can do message filtering in SNS.
So what is message filtering?
Well, it's a JSON policy that is used
to filter messages sent to the SNS topics subscription.
So if a subscription doesn't have a filter policy,
it will receive every message,
and that's a default behavior.
But let's take an example of what happens
when we set up a message filtering policy.
So we have a buying service,
and it sends transactions into an SNS topic.
For example, the transaction look like
there's an order number, there's a product, for example,
a pencil, the quantity for, and the state which is placed.
Now we want to create an SQS queue just for placed orders,
not all the orders, but just for placed orders.
So for this, we will subscribe the SQS queue
into the SNS topic, and we'll apply a filter policy in JSON,
and we will specify in a policy that we want
to have state equals placed.
And so only the message is matching the policy,
will go into the SQS queue,
But then we can have an SQS queue for canceled orders.
And so we can create our own filter policy
for canceled orders, and have those coming
from the same SNS topic into the SQS queue.
And so the placed orders and the canceled orders SQS queue
will not have the same messages.
We can also use the same filter policy, the canceled one,
to create an email subscription for canceled orders.
We could have a filter policy for declined orders,
for example, and as another SQS queue,
or we can create an SQS queue without a filter policy
to have all messages from that SNS topic.
So using all these fan out patterns
and message filtering, FIFO queues and FIFO topics,
we get lots of different possibilities/
In the exam we'll try to test you on all of those.
So that's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it,

Tutor: Let's go into a little bit more depth
on AWS step functions,
because this is a very powerful orchestration tool
and it's extremely relevant to data engineering.
So you can expect a lot of questions on this in the exam.
First, some terminology.
So the workflow that you're defining in your step functions
is called a state machine.
That's just a fancy way of saying
we have some system that defines a bunch of states
that your data pipeline might be in,
and it moves between those states somehow,
based on some criteria, right?
Every step in that workflow is called a state
because it's part of a state machine, right?
That's it, just some terminology, just some words.
However, there are many different types of states
that you can use with AWS step function.
So it is important to know these.
The most useful one is the task state.
So that is a state within your step function state machine
that does something right?
Maybe it kicks off a lambda function,
maybe it kicks off some other AWS service
to transform your data, or move it around,
or load it, or whatever it needs to do.
Maybe it even talks a third-party APIs
to do something external to AWS.
In any case, that's a task note.
It's performing some sort of real operation
on your data as you go.
There's also a choice state,
and this adds conditional logic through choice rules.
These can be things like comparisons.
You know, if my data is bigger than this amount,
maybe I do something special with it.
If this data contains PII or something,
maybe I do something special with it, right?
So choice states are just a opportunity
to apply conditional logic.
There's also a wait state
that can just be used to delay the state machine
for some specific amount of time.
If you just for whatever reason want to give things,
you know, time to catch up,
kind of a hacky way to do it,
but you can bake in a time delay
into your step functions as well with a wait state.
There's also the parallel state,
and this allows you to do separate things in parallel
and separate branches of execution.
So a parallel state isn't, well,
it's kind of a blurry concept of state, right?
It's really saying I'm gonna create many states
running in parallel at this point going on.
So I can have different things happening at the same time
once I hit a parallel state.
Now, there's also the map state,
so this can get confusing.
This is something you should probably remember.
So a map is also run in parallel,
but it says, "I'm going to run this following set of steps
for each item in a data set in parallel."
So this is especially relevant to data engineering
because it's specifically made for operating on data.
It's going to be able to work with JSON files, S3 objects,
CSV files, whatever you might have.
But it's going to take a set of steps
and apply those to that data set in parallel.
So remember, a map operation
will split things up into parallel processing on your data,
just like Apache Spark might or anything else,
and it will run in parallel
without needing a separate parallel state in front of it,
it's a parallel implicitly, okay?
So a little bit of confusing there
between parallel and map states there.
Parallel is used for kicking off separate branches
within your state machine that can do whatever,
but map is specifically about
operating on your data in a parallel way.
Finally, there's Pass, Succeed, and Fail.
Pass just passes your data along to the next step,
It's usually just used for debugging.
Succeed and Fail, though, are where you're gonna end up.
So once you're done with your state machine,
you either succeed with that state machine or fail,
and that's how you kind of wrap things up.
So that step functions in a bit more detail there.
Do remember what the valid types of states are
and what they do, it might come in handy.

# 200. Principle of Least Privilege
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40394544
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Let's dive into security,
identity, and compliance.
This is a quick one, we're gonna start off
with a very basic principle of security,
but an important one, the principle of least-privilege.
And the exam guide does say you need to know what this is.
It's pretty simple though, all it means
is that you're only granting the permissions required
for someone to perform a given task.
So it's kind of common sense, right?
Don't give people more permissions than they need
to do what they need to do, otherwise they might figure out
a way to exploit or abuse that
extraneous permission that they have.
Now, while you're developing, it certainly makes sense
to start with broader permissions,
since you don't necessarily know exactly what you need
permission for when you're still building a system
and figuring out what components make it up, right?
But once you're done, once you actually know
what somebody needs to do with that system,
you should lock it down once you have that better idea
of the exact services and operations
that a workload requires.
Over on the right, here we have an example of that.
So this is just an IAM policy that restricts S3 access
to listing a specific bucket and, furthermore,
within a specific prefix of that bucket.
So that top half there is saying,
I'm only going to allow list bucket operations
within my specific bucket under the data reports path there.
And for actually reading data, the only thing
I'm going to allow with this IAM policy is reading CSV files
that are under my specific bucket/data/reports,
and end with a .csv suffix.
So if you have, for example,
a workflow that requires people, or a system or a service,
to read CSV files from a specific location,
there's no reason to give them access
to anything more than that location.
And furthermore, just to the specific types of files
that they might need from that location, right?
So that's an example of the principle of least-privilege.
And if you're not sure what privileges you need
for an operation, you can use a tool
called the IAM Access Analyzer, and that will automatically
generate least-privilege policies,
based on the actual observed access activity.
So if while you're testing your system,
you're only doing what you're supposed to do,
you could use IAM Access Analyzer
to automatically give you a starting point
of what those least-privilege policies might look like.

And again, the syntax error
isn't something you'll be expected to know, I don't think,
but just know that you can do that.
Also, anonymization is another way of doing it.
So rather than masking something,
you can replace that data
with something that is not traceable
back to where it came from.
So you could just replace
a credit card number or a password, or whatever it is
with random information,
you could shuffle it
so that you're just shuffling everything in a given column
so that people's actual credit card numbers
don't match up to the actual person.
Another approach would be encryption,
and that can be deterministic,
where you can always get the same result
from encrypting the same input, or probabilistic,
where you might have a different result
every time you encrypt it.
Hashing is another technique
that we talked about before too,
where you just apply what's called
a hash function to the string.
And the thing with hashing
is that you might get
more than one thing that hashes to the same value,
but you know at the end,
that just increases the anonymization of it, right?
Or even better, just delete it
or don't import it in the first place.
If you don't need credit card numbers
or passwords for whatever you're doing,
don't take it, you know?
If you see that information coming in,
delete it during your ETL,
or don't even try to import it to begin with.
That's probably the safest way
of dealing with personally identifiable information,
don't have it in the first place.

# 202. Key Salting
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40394578
# Caption: en_US (auto)

-: Another technique for further improving
the security of personal or sensitive information
is something called key salting.
So if you're gonna be hashing some credit card number,
or a password or something, the idea of salting
is either appending or pre-pending some random value,
known as a salt, to the piece of data,
which might be the password, before you hash it.
This prevents people from just going through
what we call rainbow table attacks,
where they just have a list of already used passwords,
or some list of passwords
that they got from some nefarious source,
and just go through that whole table trying to find matches.
So if the passwords you're actually storing
have some sort of random information
stuck at the beginning or at the end of them,
that will thwart their attempts
to guess what those passwords are.
This ensures that the same piece of data,
like two identical passwords,
don't produce the same hash across different instances
because of that unique salt value
that was added in front of it, or at the end of it.
A best practice is to make sure your salts are strong,
cryptographically-secure random values
so nobody can try to guess what they might be,
and you also wanna rotate those salts periodically
to make it even harder.
So if somebody does crack your list of salt values,
you won't necessarily be in trouble.
You also wanna make sure that every user
has their own unique salt value.
So you don't wanna be reusing the same salt on every user.
Then, if somebody finds out what that salt value is,
you're done, right?
There's no point to that anymore.
So a better practice is to have unique salt values
for each user.
So what you wanna do is salt and then hash your passwords,
or whatever it might be, before you store them.
That way, the stored value for that password
will be a lot harder to crack
because of that random salt value that's a part of it.
Just to make this real with an example.
Let's say we have user one and user two,
and they both have the same password.
They're not very good at making passwords,
so their password is both password123.
However, they both have unique salt values,
that are random and cryptographically secure,
that are associated with each user.
So user one has one salt value,
user two has a different salt value.
And if we stick each salt value after that password string,
you can see that after we hash that
with the SHA256 algorithm,
they look completely different from each other
even though they both encode the same exact password.
So that's one little trick for being extra secure
in how you're storing
your personally identifiable information.
And as long as you know what that salt is for each user,
you can still create the same hash value
for that user's password,
and make sure they compare and match up properly
within your applications.

# 203. Preventing Backups or Replication to Disallowed AWS Regions
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40394612
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Another compliance concern
you might have is keeping data out of geographical areas
where you're not allowed to have it.
So oftentimes, you'll have restrictions
on where data can live.
Different countries have different laws about
how PII is stored, and privacy laws, and stuff like that.
So sometimes you have to be careful about
what jurisdiction you're actually storing your data in.
And it's all too easy to mistakenly,
or accidentally send data someplace where it shouldn't be.
A very common cause of this is backups or replication
where maybe you're being very well intentioned
and backing your data up to a different region
for better resilience from failures in one region.
But if you're not careful, you might end up doing
that backup or that replication someplace
where that data is not allowed to reside.
So there are some ways of enforcing that.
There's this system called AWS Organizations,
which isn't something we've really talked about,
but it's out there
and it has something called Service Control Policies.
That's one way to enforce these sorts
of geographic restrictions.
The more common way would be to just use
IAM policies and S3 bucket policies
to make sure you're locking everything down
to the regions data is allowed to be in.
So you just have to give more thought to your IAM policies
and think about not only what operations am I permitting,
but where am I permitting these things to happen?
So you need to take care, especially when you're configuring
the permissions for backups and replication for RDS,
Aurora, Redshift, or any other database, or data store.
And also you wanna set up your monitors
and alarming with CloudTrail and CloudWatch.
So if something does mistakenly go to the wrong country,
at least you'll know about it quickly
and you can take care of the situation.
Just for a real example here, here's one IAM policy
and its purpose in life is to make sure
that we're not gonna do any RDS backups outside
of the us-east-1 and us-west-1 regions.
So if you kind of study this statement over here,
we're saying that we're going to only allow
CreateDBSnapshot and CopyDBSnapshot
to the us-west-1 and us-east-1 region.
So that's restricting those backups
to just those two regions, however, we're gonna allow
everything else to happen anywhere.
So the second part of this policy says
we're gonna allow any other action
that's not CreateDBSnapshot or CopyDBSnapshot anywhere.
So this is just making sure that we're not replicating data
someplace outside of those regions,
but we can still access that data from any place.

Instructor: Welcome to the first deep dive
on an AWS service.
The first one is called IAM.
So IAM stands for the Identity and Access Management.
It is a global service
because in IAM we are going to create our users
and assign them to group.
So we've already used IAM without knowing.
When we created an account, we created a root account.
And it's been created by default,
this is the root user of our account.
And the only thing you should use it for is
to set up your account as we'll do it right now.
But then you shouldn't use
that account anymore or even share it.
What you should be doing instead is create users.
So you will create users in IAM
and one user represents one person within your organization
and the users can be grouped together if it makes sense.
So let's take an example.
We have an organization with six people.
We have Alice, Bob, Charles, David, Edward, and Fred.
So all these people are in your organization.
Now, Alice, Bob, and Charles,
they work together, they're all developers.
So we're going to create a group called the group developers
regrouping, Alice, Bob, and Charles.
And it turns out that David and Edward also work together,
so we're going to create an operations group.
Now we have two groups within IAM.
Now groups can only contain users not other groups.
So this is something very important to understand.
Groups only contain users.
Now some users don't have to belong to a group.
For example, Fred right here is alone.
He does not correspond to any group.
That is not best practice,
but it is something you can do in AWS.
And also a user can belong to multiple groups.
That means that, for example,
if you know that Charles and David work together
and they're part of your audit team,
you can create a third group with Charles and David.
And as you can see now in this example,
Charles and David are part of two different groups.
So this is the possible configurations for IAM.
So why do we create users and why do we create groups?
Well because we want to allow them to use our AWS accounts
and to allow them to do so,
we have to give them permissions.
So users are in groups can be assigned
what's called a JSON document.
I'll show you right now what it means,
called a policy, an IAM policy.
So it looks just like this.
So you don't have to be a programmer.
This is not programming.
This is just describing in I think plain English
what a user is allowed to do
or what a group and all the users within the group
are allowed to do.
So in this example,
we can see that we allow people to use the EC2 service
and do Describe on it,
to use the Elastic Load Balancing service
and do Describe on it,
and to use CloudWatch.
Now we'll see
what EC2 Elastic Load Balancing and CloudWatch mean,
but through this JSON document that looks just like this,
we are allowing our users to use some services in AWS.
So these policies will help us
define permissions of our users.
And so in AWS,
you don't allow everyone to do everything
that would be catastrophic
'cause a new user could basically launch so many services
and that will cost you a lot of money
or this would be a problem for security.
So in AWS,
you apply a principle called the least privileged principle.
So you don't give more permissions than a user needs, okay?
So if a user just needs access to three services,
just create a permission for that user.
So now we have seen an overview of IAM,
let's go in the next lecture to practice
creating users and groups.

# 207. IAM Policies
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40306592
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Okay, so now let's discuss
IAM policies in depth.
So let's imagine we have a group of developers, Alice, Bob,
and Charles, and we attach a policy at the group level.
In that case, the policy will get applied
to every single member of the group.
So both Alice, Bob, and Charles,
they will all get access and inherit this policy.
Now, if you have a second group with operations
with a different policy, David and Edward
will have a different policy than the group of developers.
If Fred is a user, it has the possibility not to belong
to a group and we have the possibility
to create what's called an inline policy,
which is a policy that's only attached to a user.
So that user could or could not belong to a group.
You can have inline policies for whatever user you want.
And finally, if Charles and David
both belong to the audit team
and you attach a policy to the audit team as well,
Charles and David will also inherit
that policy from the audit team.
So in this case, Charles has a policy from developers
and a policy from other team,
and David has a policy from other team
and a policy from the operations team.
That should make a lot of sense
when we get into the hands-on.
Now, in terms of the policy structure,
you just need to know at a high level how it works
as well as how it is named.
So this is something you will see quite a lot in AWS.
So get familiar with this structure.
This is adjacent documents.
And so an IAM policy structure consists of a version number.
So usually it's 2012-10-17,
this is the policy language version, an ID,
which is how to identify that policy, this is optional.
And then more statements and statements
can be one or multiple ones.
And a statement has some very important parts.
So the SID is the statement ID, which is an identifier
for the statement, which is optional as well.
So on the right-hand side is the number one,
the effect of the policy itself.
So it is whether or not the statement allows
or denies access to certain APIs.
So in the right-hand side, this is allow,
but you can see deny as well.
The principle consists of which account user
or role to which this policy will be applied to.
So in this example, it's applied to the root accounts
of your AWS accounts.
Action is the list of API calls that will be either denied
or allowed based on the effects.
And the resource is a list of resources
to which the actions will be applied to.
So in this example, it is a bucket,
but it could be many different things.
And finally, in not represented here,
but there's a condition to which when this statement
should be applied or not.
And this is not represented here because it is optional.
So going into the exam, you need to make sure
that you really understand the effect,
the principle, the action, and resource.
But don't worry, you'll see those
along the way in the course.
So you should be confident
with them by the end of the course.
That's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 209. IAM MFA
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40306602
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now that we have created users in groups,
it is time for us to protect these users
in groups from being compromised.
So for this, we have two defense mechanisms.
The first one is to define
what's called a password policy.
Why?
Well, because the stronger the password you use,
the more security for your accounts.
So in AWS you can set up a password policy
with different options.
The first one is you can set a minimum
password length and you can
require specific character types.
For example, you may want
to have an uppercase letter, lowercase letter,
number, non alphanumeric characters,
for example, a question mark and so on.
Then you can allow or not IAM users
to change their own passwords,
or you can require users to change their password
after some time to make your password expired,
for example, to say every 90 days,
users have to change their passwords.
Finally, you can also prevent password reuse
so that users, when they change their passwords,
don't change it to the one
that they already have or change it
to the one they had before.
So this is great.
A password policy really is helpful
against brute force attacks on your account.
But there's a second defense mechanism
that you need to know going into the exam.
And this is the Multi-Factor Authentication or MFA.
It is possible, you already used it
on some websites, but on AWS it's a must
and it's very recommended to use it.
So users have access to your account
and they can possibly do a lot of things,
especially if they're administrators.
They can change configuration,
delete resources and other things.
So you absolutely want to protect
at least your root account and hopefully,
all your IAM users.
So how do we protect them on top of the password?
Well, you use an MFA device.
So what is MFA?
MFA is using the combination of a password
that you know and a security device that you own.
And these two things together
have a much greater security
than just a password.
So for example, let's take Alice.
Alice knows her password,
but she also has an MFA generating token.
And by using these things together
while logging in, she's going to be able
to do a successful login on MFA.
So the benefit of MFA is that even if Alice
has lost her password
because it's stolen or it's hacked,
the account will not be compromised
because the hacker will need to also get a hold
of the physical device of Alice,
that could be her phone, for example,
to do a login.
Obviously that is much less likely.
So what are the MFA devices option in AWS?
And you need to know them going into the exam,
but don't worry, they're quite simple.
The first one is a virtual MFA device.
This is what we'll be using in the hands-on.
And so you can use Google Authenticator,
which is just working on one phone at a time,
or using Authy.
So for Authy, you have support
for multiple tokens on a single device.
So that means that with the virtual MFA device,
you can have your root account,
your IAM user, another account, another IAM user.
It's up to you.
You can have as many users and accounts
as you want on your virtual MFA device,
which make it a very easy solution to use.
Now we have another thing
called a Universal 2nd Factor
or U2F Security Key,
and that is a physical device.
For example, a YubiKey by Yubico
and Yubico is a third party to AWS.
This is not AWS that provides it.
This is a third party.
And we use a physical device
because maybe it's super easy,
you put it on your key fobs
and you're good to go.
So this YubiKey supports multiple root
and IAM users using a single security key.
So you don't need as many keys as users,
otherwise there will be a nightmare.
Then you have other options.
You have a hardware key fob MFA device,
for example, this one provided by Gemalto,
which is also a third party to AWS.
And finally, if you are using the cloud
of the government in the US, the AWS GovCloud,
then you have a special key fob
that looks like this
that is provided by SurePassID,
which is also a third party.
So that's it.
We've seen the theory
on how to protect your account,
but let's go in the next lecture
to implement that.
So I will see you in the next lecture.

# 213. Encryption 101
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40306618
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: Okay, so in this lecture,
if you're not too familiar with how encryption works,
I want to give you a little bit of details
on how it works at a high level.
So first, let's talk about encryption in flight,
which is going to be referred as TLS or SSL.
TLS is the newest version of SSL.
So what we have is that the data is going to be encrypted
before sending the data,
and then it will be decrypted after receiving it.
So this is for communication between a client
and a server over a network.
And so what's going to be happening is that
for encrypting the data,
TLS certificates are going to be used.
And this is what you see when you go onto websites
and it says HTTPS, that means that the connection
between you and the server is going to be encrypted
using TLS certificates.
Why do we want encryption in flight?
Well, because we're sending data over a network,
and sometimes a public network,
and the data goes around many different servers.
We don't want to be having a man-in-the-middle attacks
where a middle server receive the data
and just observe the packages we're sending to the server.
This is why we want to have HTTPS or TLS or SSL.
This is when we know
that only the target server can decrypt
the encrypted data we're sending.
So let's take an example.
We have a client and a server,
and we want to be able to securely log in into the server
by providing our username and password,
but we only want the target server to be able to receive it.
So we're going to have the username and password,
and then we're going to apply TLS encryption
on the client-side automatically.
The data is going to be encrypted
and sent over the network.
So as you can see, no between server can decrypt the data,
and only the target server can use the TLS
decryption mechanism to decrypt that package
and then see that we've sent the username and password,
and therefore say that we're securely logged in.
So that's for encryption in flight.
The next one is around server-side encryption at rest.
The idea is that the data will be encrypted
after being received by the server
so that it's stored securely.
And the data will be decrypted
before being sent back to our clients.
It will be stored in an encrypted form, thanks to a key,
and the key is usually a data key.
And so the whole idea of managing these keys
for encryption and encryption is that the management
must happen somewhere,
and the server must have access to these keys.
So let's take a service, for example, Amazon S3.
We're sending an object over HTTP, maybe even HTTPS
for infra-encryption.
And so the service receives our object, but it is decrypted.
So the service can use a data key.
And using the data key and the decrypted object,
we can have encryption of that object at rest.
And then when it comes to sending back that object
to the client,
the encrypted object and the data key
will be used together to decrypt,
will have a decrypted form of object,
and then that object will be sent over HTTPS
back to the clients
so we receive the decrypted object as-is.
As we can see in this case,
there is a server-side encryption because all the encryption
and decryption happens on the server.
So finally, let's talk about client-side encryption.
And the idea is that this time the data is encrypted
and decrypted at the client-side,
and the server should never be able to decrypt the data
because we don't trust the server in that case.
So for this we could leverage
envelope encryption for this mechanism.
So let's have an example.
The client has an object,
and the data key this time is client-side.
And after encryption, we get an encrypted object.
That encrypted objects can be sent then securely
to any storage service, for example, an FTP server,
Amazon S3, EBS Volume, et cetera,
and it will be stored in encrypted form.
So the target server cannot even decrypt the data content.
When we retrieve the content,
we retrieve the encrypted object directly.
And if we still have access to the data key client-side,
then we're able to perform the decryption mechanism
and get the decrypted object back.
So that's it for the three encryption mechanisms
we can see in the cloud.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 214. AWS KMS
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40306620
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS KMS,
which is a key management service of AWS.
So we've been using it a lot without knowing,
but anytime you hear encryption
when you have an AWS service,
it's most likely going to be KMS encryption.
The aim is that with this KMS service,
AWS is going to manage the encryption keys for us.
And that's great,
because that means that we have less things to do.
So KMS is, of course,
fully integrated with IAM for authorization,
and it gives us very easy ways to control access
to our data if it's encrypted with KMS.
The power of using AWS KMS is that you're able
to audit every single API call made to use your keys
through CloudTrail,
which is something the exam may test you on.
So on top of it,
KMS can be used seamlessly into most AWS services.
So for example, if you wanted to encrypt the data at rest
in an EBS volume, just enable the KMS integration.
Same for S3, same for RDS, same for SSM,
and same for pretty much all the services
that require encryption.
The idea is that with KMS, you can also use it yourself.
And if you have secrets data,
you never ever store them in plain text,
that means just as is.
Especially in your code.
So if you want to use KMS,
you can also use KMS through API calls.
You can use the AWS CLI or the SDK.
And that means that you can encrypt
whatever is a secret for you with a KMS key.
And then these encrypted secrets can be, for example,
stored in your code or in environment variables.
That is a much better pattern.
So now let's talk about the different types
of KMS keys available to you.
So now it's called a KMS key.
By the way, it used to be called
the KMS customer master key, but it was confusing
because there's also the customer managed keys
as we'll see in a second.
So now, we just talk about KMS keys.
So we have two types of KMS keys.
We have the symmetric KMS keys,
and that means there's only one single encrypted key
that is used to encrypt and decrypt data.
And so any service of AWS that is integrated
with KMS will use symmetric keys.
The idea is that when we create or use a KMS symmetric key,
then we never get access to the key itself, okay?
All we do is that we use the KMS API calls
to leverage and use that key.
The second kind of key available on KMS
are called asymmetric keys.
That means that you have two keys.
You have a public key that's used to encrypt data,
and a private key used to decrypt data.
So this is used when you have encrypt/decrypt,
or sign/verify type of operations.
And in that case,
you can download the public key out of KMS,
but you can use access the private key.
You can only use API calls
against to access the private key.
So the use cases for an asymmetric type of key
is when you want the encryption to be done outside
of your AWS cloud by users who cannot
or don't have access to the KMS API key.
In which case they will use the public key
to encrypt the data.
Send it over to you.
And you within your account,
you would use the private key of AWS to decrypt that data.
So within the world of KMS keys,
you have different types of KMS keys.
The first one are AWS owned keys.
They're free, and this is the kind of key you would use
when you use SSE-S3 type of encryption,
or SSC DynamoDB, where you have the option, for example,
that you choose a key owned by DynamoDB.
So these are not really KMS
because you don't really see them,
but they're types of encryption keys within AWS.
Then you have the AWS managed keys, and they're free,
and you will recognize them
because they start with AWS slash and then the service name.
For example, AWS/RDS or AWS/EBS,
or in this example, AWS/DynamoDB.
They're free and you can just use them as you please,
but only from within the service that it's assigned to.
Then you have your own customer managed keys
and their custom keys, and they cost you $1 per month.
And if you want to import them as well, you can import them,
and they cost you $1 per month.
KMS also has a pricing where you're going to pay
for each API call made to the KMS service,
which is about 3 cents per 10,000 API calls.
You also have automatic key rotation.
So if it's an AWS managed KMS key,
then it's automatic every one year.
And if it's a customer managed key,
you can enable automatic rotation and you set the period,
and you can also have on-demand rotation of your key.
And if it's imported KMS key,
then you can only manually rotate it.
And for this, you need to leverage an alias.
So KMS keys are scoped per region.
That means that if you have an EBS volume encrypted
with KMS key in a region, for example, EUS2,
then if you want to copy that to a different region,
we have to do several steps.
First of all, we have to take a snapshot of this EBS volume.
And if we take a snapshot from an encrypted snapshot,
then this snapshot itself will also be encrypted
with the same KMS key.
Then to copy the snapshot to another region,
we need to re-encrypt the snapshot using
a different KMS key.
And this is something AWS will do for you.
But the same KMS key cannot live in two regions.
So now we have an EBS snapshot,
it's encrypted with KMS with a different key,
and it lives in another region.
Now, we restore the snapshot
into its own EBS volume with KMS,
and it's KMS key B into the region AP southeast two.
Now, the other thing we need
to know about is KMS key policies.
So this is to control access to your KMS keys.
It's similar to an S3 bucket policy.
With a difference that if you don't have the KMS key policy
on your KMS key, then no one can access it.
So in that regards, we have two types of KMS key policies.
We have the default one,
and it's created if you don't provide
a specific custom KMS key policy.
And the idea is that the default allows
everyone in your account to access this key.
That means that if you have an IAM policy allowing a user
or role to access this key policy, you're good.
But if you want to have more specific controls over it,
you could use a KMS key policy that is custom.
In which you define the users,
the roles that can access your KMS key.
And you define who can administer the key.
And this is especially helpful
if you want to do cross account access for your KMS key,
because we can authorize another account to use our KMS key.
So when do we use this?
Well, for example,
if we wanted to copy an encrypted snapshots across accounts.
So we create a snapshot encrypted with our own KMS key,
and it's a customer managed key.
It must be that because we need
to attach a custom key policy.
And then we attach a KMS key policy
to authorize for cross account access.
It looks like this.
Then we share the encrypted snapshot
with the target account.
And then in the target account,
we create a copy of the snapshot
and we encrypt it with a different customer managed key
in that target account.
And then we can create a volume from the snapshot
in the target account, and we're done.
So that's a lot of information by KMS,
but let's go into hands-on
to hopefully learn a bit more about it.

# 219. AWS WAF
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40306650
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: So now, let's talk about AWS WAF,
the web application firewall.
It's used to protect your web application
from common web exploits at the layer seven.
Just a reminder, layer seven is HTTP,
so it protects you against HTTP exploits,
whereas, as comparison,
layer four is for TCP or UDP protocol.
So this WAF, this web application firewall,
can be deployed on the application balancer,
an API gateway, CloudFront, the AppSync GraphQL API,
or Cognito User Pools.
So remember, this is very important you remember
the targets of WAF because the exam will try to trick you
and for example, make you deploy WAF on an NLB,
but this is not possible.
So once you've deployed a firewall on these services,
you can define Web ACL, their web access control lists.
And their rules, and so you can set a rule, for example,
to filter based on IP addresses.
So you can define an IP sets.
Each IP set can be up to 10,000 IP addresses.
And if you need more IP addresses,
you can use multiple rules for more IPs.
You can also filter based on HTTP headers, body,
you can use URI strings to protect
from the most common attacks such as SQL injection
and cross-site scripting,
you can have size constraints to make sure
that the requests are only up to, for example,
two megabytes, or geo-match to allow
or block specific countries,
and you can even have rate-based rules
to count the occurrences of requests per IP
for DDoS protection, for example, to prevent a specific IP
from sending more than 10 requests per second.
So these Web ACLs, they're regional except for CloudFront
where they are defined globally.
And if you see the term rule group, well it's a set,
it's a reasonable set of rules that you can add
to many Web ACL.
So this is just to organize them.
So WAF has a really good use case.
So what if you want to get a fixed IP
on our application while using WAF
with a application load balancer?
So WAF does not support the network load balancer
because the NLB operates on layer four
and WAF is for layer seven.
So therefore, to provide WAF,
you need to have an application load balancer.
But we know that an application load balancer
does not have fixed IPs.
So to solve a problem, we can use a global accelerator
to get fixed IP for application
and then enable WAF on our ALB.
So the architecture is like this.
We have one region with an ALB and EC2 instances,
we're going to front our ALB with a global accelerator
to get a fixed IP for our application,
and we're going to attach a web application firewall
with a Web ACL on the same region
as where our application load balancer is located.
And therefore, we have achieved our target architecture.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

What is DDoS?
Well, it's a Distributed Denial of Service
and the idea is that your infrastructure is going
to suddenly receive many,
many requests at the same time from a lot
of computers all around the world.
And so the goal of it is to overwhelm
and overload your infrastructure.
And this way your infrastructure cannot
serve your real users.
And this is what it's called
a Distributed Denial of Service.
So we can protect against it.
So we have the AWS Shield Standard service.
It's a free service, it's already activated
for every customer of AWS.
And it's going to give you protection from attacks such
as the SYN or UDP Floods
or any Reflection attack
or other Layer Three or Layer Four attacks.
And if you want to get advanced protection,
you can use the AWS Shield Advanced service.
So this is an optional DDoS mitigation service.

to get protected against more sophisticated
DDoS attacks on Amazon EC2,
Elastic Load Balancing,
Amazon CloudFront,
Global Accelerator, and Route 53.
It also gives you access, 24/7 access,
to the AWS DDoS response team.

fees because you are also being attacked,

DDoS attacks if they happen at

# Section: Networking and Content Delivery

Okay, so now let's talk about
how we can establish connectivity
between VPC and other structures.
So, the first thing is called VPC peering.
So say you have two virtual private clouds,
they're either in two different accounts
or in two different regions,
and you want to connect together
as if they're part of the same network.
So we want to connect to VPC privately
using the network from AWS.
And it's going to make them behave
as if they were in the same network,
so we have VPC A and VPC B,
and if we want to have them talk to one another,
we need to establish a VPC peering connection from A to B.
Very simple.
To make sure that these VPC can be connected,
you need to make sure that the IP ranges
that is defined for each VPC are not overlapping.
Because to be able to address network to another VPC,
you need to talk to an IP address.
And so, if obviously, the network ranges overlap,
then the network doesn't know where to go.
So to connect to VPC, you need to make sure
that the IP addresses range it operates on
are different and not overlapping.
And a VPC peering connection is not transitive.
So it must be established for each VPC
that needs to communicate with one another.
What I mean is that if we connect VPC C
through a VPC peering connection between A and C,
B and C cannot talk to each other.
There is no transitivity in the VPC peering.
That means that if I want to establish connectivity
between VPC B and VPC C,
then I need to create its own
VPC peering connection between B and C.
That's what it means with VPC peering.
So as you add more and more VPC,
you need to add more and more peering connections.
Okay, that's number one.
Number two, VPC endpoints,
which is going to be very important going into this exam.

to AWS services using a private network
instead of using the public internet network.

And so anytime your EC2 instances, for example,

privately, your AWS services.

But so, your EC2 instance talks to that VPC endpoint

As you can see,
the traffic does not go through the internet.
And then, for VPC endpoint interface,

and that's only used within your VPC,

Therefore, you need to establish VPC peering connections
between all your VPC
if you want to have them connected with each other.
VPC Endpoints is going to provide you private access
to AWS Services within your VPC, and that is something
that we will see in the future lectures for some services.
And VPC Flow Logs will give you your network traffic log
to ensure that you can debug if something is access denied,
if traffic is blocked or allowed within your VPC.
Finally, to establish connection
from your on-premises data center to AWS,
you have the Site to Site VPN,
which is to have a VPN connection over the public internet.
And your Direct Connect, if it's,
you want a direct private connection to AWS.

# 229. AWS PrivateLink
# Section: Networking and Content Delivery
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-data-engineer/learn/lecture/40306890
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Instructor: So now let's talk about AWS PrivateLink
also from the VPC Endpoint Services family.
So how does that work?
Well, say you have a service that you run within AWS
or say there is a vendor on the marketplace
and they run a service on their own accounts
within their own VPC and they want to expose a service
to customers of AWS.
So to thousands of VPC,
they need to have private access to that service
to establish a connectivity.
You could, for example, use VPC peering,
but that doesn't scale and it's not very secure.
What you want is use something else,
and that's something else is a PrivateLink.
So a PrivateLink allows you to connect a service
running within your VPC
to other VPCs directly and privately.
So it does not require VPC peering or internet gateway
because it's from the private network, or NAT,
or route tables or anything like this.
So let's go through diagrams.
Say, for example, you are talking to a vendor
on the AWS marketplace
and they run application service
so they have their own service that you want to use
in their own VPC
and you want to have access to it from your own VPC
in your own accounts with your own consumer applications.
In that case, you're going to ask your vendor
to do a Private Link.
On their end, they will have to create
a network load balancer to expose that service,
and on your end,
you will create an elastic network interface
and then you will establish a Private Link between the two
so that you have private access
to their network load balancer
and therefore to their service.
And all the internet traffic is actually not gonna go
through the public internet,
but it's actually gonna go through your private network,
and so therefore all communications will remain private.
And so for every new customer
that that third party will need,
all they will have to do is to create a new Private Link
for their customers,
which is very easy to manage and way more scalable.

Top level domains, which is .com, .us, .in, .gov,
.org, et cetera, et cetera.
Second level domain, which is amazon.com and google.com.

we have http://api.www.example.com., okay?

Then the .com so.com is your TLD.
So that's your top level domain.

api.www.example.com is your FQDN,
your fully qualified domain name,
HTP is going to be your protocol.

So now that we know a little bit of terminology,

So we have a web server,

hey, do you know what example.com is?

and managed by your company

has never seen this query before,
what it's going to do
is first ask the root DNS server managed
by the I C A N N, the ICANN organization,
and it's going to say, hey, do you know what's example.com?

and the root DNS server is going to say,

hey, I don't have this answer,

So the local DNS server saying, okay, good.
Now I'm going to ask the top level domain.

I'm going to ask for the answer of my query.

and the example.com okay, is going to be asked again
to this DNS server.
So do you know about example.com

I don't know about example but I do know about example.com.

which is at 5.6.7.8.
That's a public IP that you should ask the answer

So the local DNS server is then going to go
to our final server,
which is the sublevel domain DNS server.
And this is a server that is going to be managed
by your domain registrar.
So it could be, for example, Amazon Route 53 and so on.
So the DNS server is gonna say,
hey, do you know about example.com?

and it turns out that example.com,
I know that it's an a record and that the result

and then it says, okay, hey, yes, I'm going to cache
